Daybreak Red is now available in AWS GovCloud (US-East)

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (286 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that building on the availability of Daybreak models on Amazon Bedrock, GPT‑5.6 Cyber is now available to approved customers in AWS GovCloud (US-East)⁠(opens in a upcoming window) through Daybreak Red.
  • It has been revealed that daybreak Red provides access to OpenAI’s purpose-trained cybersecurity models for authorized vulnerability research, exploit validation, and security testing.
  • For government organizations, adopting advanced cybersecurity capabilities requires more than model performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that building on the availability of Daybreak models on Amazon Bedrock, GPT‑5.6 Cyber is now available to approved customers in AWS GovCloud (US-East)⁠(opens in a upcoming window) through Daybreak Red. This expansion gives government security teams a new way to apply advanced cybersecurity capabilities within the AWS environments they use to support critical missions.

It has been revealed that daybreak Red provides access to OpenAI’s purpose-trained cybersecurity models for authorized vulnerability research, exploit validation, and security testing. GPT‑5.6 Cyber can help defenders investigate complex software weaknesses, reproduce vulnerabilities in controlled settings, and develop mitigations. Qualified security practitioners should review findings and proposed fixes before implementation.

For government organizations, adopting advanced cybersecurity capabilities requires more than model performance. Teams also need to work within established security, governance, and operational requirements.

Availability in AWS GovCloud (US-East) gives eligible teams a path to incorporate GPT‑5.6 Cyber into those workflows through Amazon Bedrock. Defenders can use it to reason through security findings, assess their impact, and evaluate fixes, helping connect vulnerability research to practical improvements in defense.

Daybreak Red gives verified defenders greater latitude for authorized cybersecurity work, with fewer refusals for these tasks alongside stronger identity verification, monitoring, and access controls.

For Daybreak Red on Amazon Bedrock, inference data is not used to train models, and customers do not need to share their Daybreak Red data with OpenAI.

Access requires OpenAI Daybreak Red approval and AWS provisioning. To get started, complete the Daybreak application or contact your OpenAI or AWS account team about eligibility. Once approved, work with your AWS account team to enable access. Daybreak Red approval does not automatically enable model access on AWS.

Learn more about Daybreak models on AWS.

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: OpenAI to acquire Pierre Computer Tech giant, Inc.

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (472 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Expanding Codex’s tools for building, understanding, and reviewing code.
  • According to recent reports, today we're announcing that OpenAI will acquire Pierre Computer Manufacturer, Inc⁠(opens in a new window).
  • We’ve seen in our own engineering work how the systems around Git need to evolve as more of that work happens in parallel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Expanding Codex’s tools for building, understanding, and reviewing code.

According to recent reports, today we're announcing that OpenAI will acquire Pierre Computer Manufacturer, Inc⁠(opens in a new window). (“Pierre”), the company behind Code Storage⁠(opens in a new window) and a family of standout open-source developer tools. If you’ve browsed files or reviewed a change in the Codex app, you’ve already used Pierre’s Trees and Diffs libraries. We’re excited to work with the Pierre team to build on the Git workflows that developers already rely on and adapt them to how teams work with coding agents.

We’ve seen in our own engineering work how the systems around Git need to evolve as more of that work happens in parallel. Earlier this week, we shared how we’re scaling Git at OpenAI with Pando, our in-house source control backend for engineers and agents. With the Pierre team, we wish to set the standard for modern software development: from the first branch an agent creates to that magic moment when code is deployed to the world. We want to make Codex the place where developers and agents take on their most ambitious projects.

According to recent reports, we’ve long appreciated the care Pierre brings to another part of working with Git: how developers review code. You can see that care in the libraries we use in Codex today. Trees lets developers promptly navigate a project’s files, and Diffs makes it easy to see what changed. Both of these tools make it easy to review and navigate large volumes of code with uncompromising performance.

Industry observers note that that same attention to detail runs through Pierre’s other work. Diffs’ Edit mode lets a reviewer fix a line of code right where they spot the problem. Pierre recently released Highlights, an extremely fast syntax highlighter that updates as a developer types or an agent streams code. The same small team that put an editor inside a diff also designed the API for Code Storage, a service that lets apps store code and track its history using Git.

Recent findings suggest that pierre has built tools that developers love, and together, we will ship new products and platforms that benefit all. Once the acquisition closes, our ambition is to advance the future of source control across the industry. We want Codex to connect the code a company ships with the decisions its people make, at the scale the future demands.

Recent findings suggest that pierre’s open-source projects will remain open-source, and we’ll continue to contribute to them. Customers can continue using Code Storage after the acquisition closes while we work to bring its features and functionality into Codex.

The closing of the acquisition is subject to customary closing conditions, including receipt of regulatory approvals. Until closing, OpenAI and Pierre will remain separate and independent companies.

#18873. Franklin Templeton uses OpenAI to support investment research

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (746 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Franklin Templeton uses OpenAI to support investment research

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (746 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Starting with equity research, Franklin Templeton is developing AI workflows to help portfolio managers compare views and examine risks.
  • In a recent development, franklin Templeton wants AI to help portfolio managers examine different research views and the risks behind an investment idea.
  • When Franklin Templeton first tried using AI, the team put data in a database and connected the models to it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Starting with equity research, Franklin Templeton is developing AI workflows to help portfolio managers compare views and examine risks.

In a recent development, franklin Templeton wants AI to help portfolio managers examine different research views and the risks behind an investment idea. Codex is one of several tools our investment teams are using to develop workflows for investment research.

When Franklin Templeton first tried using AI, the team put data in a database and connected the models to it. But it didn’t produce the answers the teams needed because the models didn’t understand how the data fit together. When the team added agents and a semantic layer, a structured model of what the firm’s data means and how it’s connected, the results changed. The team is using Codex and other tools to develop this connected intelligence layer. "We've been able to build what we think of as a connected intelligence layer," Dudley notes. "We're bringing the data into the tools, and we're surfacing insights that make a difference.".

Research, risk, compliance, and trading offer different perspectives on an investment. Franklin Templeton’s ambition is to bring those inputs together for portfolio managers. “We're able to bring that all in and then use that to surface insights to the people who are making decisions, which are our portfolio managers,” Dudley indicates.

It has been revealed that dudley describes the earlier equity-research workflow as human-led and sequential: an analyst performs first-pass stock analysis, reviews earnings calls, and studies competitors in each business line. The goal is to surface useful information as analysts prepare fresh ideas to be pitched to portfolio managers or provide updates on existing positions in the portfolio. As she puts it, “It's just continuous intelligence combined with that human judgment.”.

In the workflow Franklin Templeton envisions, its investment teams will have access to a governed, reusable intelligence foundation that brings together trusted connectors, portfolio and workflow context, and agentic capabilities that surface actionable insights for its analysts and portfolio managers.

It has been revealed that franklin Templeton has used Codex in hackathons, bringing experts alongside investment practitioners as they develop their own tools. Its Investment AI champions are working to turn experiments into production-ready workflows, with security review, expert support, and data controls as part of that process.

Dudley says, “We have moved from augmenting our research process to reimagining the investment research workflow.”.

Some of what makes AI helpful in other settings doesn't work in asset management. Many tools learn a user's preferences and show them more of the same, so if someone favors one research provider, the tool surfaces more of that provider's reports. For an investment team, that narrowing potentially brings a biased perspective into the investment process. Franklin Templeton wants the opposite. "We want to make sure that they're accessing that diversity of research and diversity of opinion," Dudley says.

Franklin Templeton wants its AI systems to emphasize investment risks. “We need AI to understand that a great investment idea is one that is well reasoned, but it also has analyzed the risks and makes our portfolio managers aware of the risk,” Dudley says. “If you’re looking at a research note, focusing on the fact someone has identified the investment risks is not a bad thing from our perspective. It makes for a more informed investment decision.”.

Franklin Templeton's experience points to some investment management best practices:.

“Our message from leadership is consistent: we encourage innovation and experimentation with AI within clearly defined risk guardrails. Not every initiative will succeed, but each should generate insights that strengthen our capabilities, inform future decisions, and drive continuous improvement,” Dudley says.

Get new tools into people's hands: Dudley states Franklin Templeton has brought practical labs to teams promptly after new technology launches, so they can test how it fits their work.

Help teams learn the tools: Dudley says, "The goal is getting them to actually understand the power of the technology.".

Build with appropriate controls: Security review, expert support, and data agreements are part of Franklin Templeton’s path from experimentation toward production-grade tools.

Dudley’s longer-term goal is to make that connected intelligence accessible across investment teams, from analysts to the leaders of each investment group.

Sources indicate that she wants analysts to spend more time in the field, speaking with many different experts and professionals, including executives at private companies, and bringing what they learn back to their investment teams. For Dudley, that human perspective remains essential as the tools develop.

Industry News: Flipsnack grows product signups with conversion optimization

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Flipsnack focused its ChatGPT Ads campaigns on getting people to try its product, growing registrations while lowering the cost per signup.
  • lower cost per registration in five US conversion-focused campaigns than in their earlier click-focused versions, which used fixed bids.¹.
  • more registrations in those same five conversion-focused campaigns compared with their earlier click-focused versions.¹.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Flipsnack focused its ChatGPT Ads campaigns on getting people to try its product, growing registrations while lowering the cost per signup.

lower cost per registration in five US conversion-focused campaigns than in their earlier click-focused versions, which used fixed bids.¹.

more registrations in those same five conversion-focused campaigns compared with their earlier click-focused versions.¹.

Recent findings suggest that flipsnack⁠(opens in a new window) helps teams turn static documents into interactive digital experiences. Its customers use the platform to create product catalogs, sales presentations, brochures, internal communications, and training materials.

Sources indicate that for Flipsnack, that range of applications creates a marketing challenge: helping people recognize how the product fits the work they need to do. As the firm increased its focus on business customers, it wanted to reach people with needs that its product category alone might not clearly describe.

Flipsnack had relied heavily on search advertising. Its ChatGPT Ads test became an opportunity to learn which customer needs could translate into product signups.

It has been revealed that because Flipsnack is a visual product, prospective customers often want to experience it before speaking with sales. Its campaign landing pages directed people into a signup flow, making completed registration the first meaningful step the team could measure and optimize for.

Industry observers note that to help business customers see where the product could fit their work, Flipsnack expanded beyond its original, broader Flipbook campaign. Separate campaigns for Magazine, Catalog, and Brochure addressed specific document needs, while campaigns for Sales Enablement, Employee Benefits, Real Estate, and Hospitality connected the product to business applications and industries.

“A sales team and an internal communications team can use the same product for very different jobs. We want our campaigns to help each see where Flipsnack fits.”.

In a recent development, flipsnack’s initial click-focused campaigns brought in traffic and signups. After seeing better delivery and registration efficiency in conversion-focused campaigns, the team rebuilt existing campaigns with a conversions objective and bidding set to maximize conversions.

Flipsnack created conversion-focused versions of five existing US campaigns that had used a clicks objective with fixed bids.

Sources indicate that early results following the shift to conversion-focused campaigns were encouraging. Across five campaigns, registrations increased approximately 310% while cost per registration fell approximately 75%, with daily budget settings unchanged.1.

Recent findings suggest that “What stood out was that we were getting more registrations at a lower cost per signup. That gave us the confidence to make conversion optimization the focus of our campaigns.”.

According to recent reports, these results give Flipsnack a promising foundation for continued growth with ChatGPT Ads. Building on its conversion-focused campaigns, the team aims to bring more prospective customers into the product and help them discover how Flipsnack can support their business.

Reach people as they explore options, compare choices, and make decisions in ChatGPT, with relevant ads that fit naturally into the experience.

Results are based on Flipsnack’s ChatGPT Ads Manager data for five US campaign pairs, August 25–31 versus September 2–8, 2026, checked September 11. Attribution uses 30-day clicks, excluding views. Daily budget limits were unchanged; spend rose approximately 1.3%. Objectives and bidding changed together.

Tech Report: Setting a latest standard for responsible AI infrastructure

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1002 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New commitments to the communities where we build and policy proposals to help more Americans share in the benefits.
  • It has been revealed that the promise of AI is that it gives people more power to shape their own futures.
  • In a recent development, the communities that host this infrastructure should have a clear say in shaping their futures, too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New commitments to the communities where we build and policy proposals to help more Americans share in the benefits.

It has been revealed that the promise of AI is that it gives people more power to shape their own futures. It can help someone learn a upcoming skill, build a business, or solve a problem that was previously out of reach. Building more computing infrastructure capacity in the United States can help lower the cost of delivering AI, put these tools in more people’s hands, and ensure America stays at the forefront of the technology.

In a recent development, the communities that host this infrastructure should have a clear say in shaping their futures, too. Residents should be able to influence how a campus is developed, hold developers accountable for covering the cost of powering it, and share in the jobs and business opportunities it creates. How we build these campuses is one of the first tests of whether the benefits of AI will be broadly shared.

Today we’re publishing our National Community Compact⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) and a Compute Campus Policy Blueprint⁠(opens in a new window). The compact sets out what communities can expect from OpenAI at future campuses that we own and operate. The blueprint proposes policies to help ensure that compute campus development gives communities a meaningful voice, protects families from new costs, and broadly shares the economic gains of AI.

This builds on work we began in January, when we declared our Stargate Community commitments to pay our own way on energy and develop looks shaped by local priorities. We followed with specific commitments in Georgia and Ohio, covering energy costs, water use, local investment and accountability. Throughout that work, we’ve listened to residents, local leaders, schools and businesses about what matters to their communities. Today’s announcement is the next step in that ongoing effort.

Recent findings suggest that every future compute campus OpenAI owns and operates will have its own local compact. We’ll engage residents early enough to ensure their input shapes project prepares, give them a local point of contact throughout the life of the campus, and report publicly each year on how we’re doing. Each compact will reflect local priorities and include a common set of commitments:.

Recent findings suggest that pay our own way on energy and infrastructure. We’ll pay the full cost of the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve us. Before major spending begins, we’ll provide financial assurances so other customers are protected if a project is delayed, reduced, or canceled.

Recent findings suggest that protect local resources and report on our impact. We’ll develop a water plan for each campus, prioritize closed-loop or low-water cooling, and publish site-level water and electricity use. We’ll publish construction plans and independent noise studies before operations begin and annually afterward. And we will not use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials, allowing only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.

In a recent development, create opportunities for local workers and businesses. We’ll publish the jobs we expect to create, work with unions and training providers to help residents prepare for them, and report annually on hiring and apprenticeships. We’ll also make sustained investments in priorities residents help select.

Those priorities will differ from place to place. In Effingham County, Georgia, residents helped shape a $4.8 million grant to provide free school meals for all 14,000 students in the county. In Pike County, Ohio, families identified childcare as a priority, leading to a joint $6 million commitment from OpenAI and SB Energy.

Industry observers note that families should be able to count on basic protections whoever builds a campus in their community. Voluntary commitments from companies are an important starting point, but our blueprint goes further—asking federal, state, and local policymakers to establish clear rules for how the industry builds. New policy is required to establish trust and confidence between communities, elected officials and companies. Lawmakers should establish rules to advance responsible investment, protect residents, and ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared.

That starts with who pays for power. State utility commissions should require large electricity customers to cover the costs they add to the grid and protect other customers if a project falls through. Utilities should also make it easier for campuses to connect if they can safely cut demand when power is scarce. At our planned Effingham County campus, for example, our agreement with Georgia Power allows the utility to reduce the power it delivers to us by up to 1,000 megawatts during periods of high demand. Congress can help meet growing demand by speeding up transmission upgrades and restoring and expanding tax incentives for clean electricity.

Communities also need a way to hold developers accountable. The blueprint calls for public reporting on water, energy, noise, and hiring, and for narrow limits on when developers can require public officials to sign NDAs. When states or local governments offer tax incentives, the terms should be public, with measurable commitments and a way to recover benefits if a developer falls short.

Finally, the blueprint proposes practical ways to keep more of the work local to ensure compute campuses support local workers and local businesses. Developers can share purchasing plans early enough for local suppliers to compete for contracts. Employers, building trades unions, and community colleges can use hiring forecasts to train residents for jobs they know will be available, from electrical work during construction to maintaining power and cooling systems for years afterward.

It has been revealed that the investments that help America compete globally can also help communities prosper locally. That starts with giving residents a say while plans can still change and a way to hold developers accountable for delivering on their commitments. That’s what we’re committing to at the campuses we own and operate, and what we believe people should be able to count on wherever AI infrastructure is built across the country.

Merge builds product and business tools with OpenAI technology

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The integration platform uses GPT‑6 Astra, ChatGPT, and Codex for product reviews, marketing, and business development planning.
  • According to recent reports, merge helps companies build connected software and AI products, from syncing customer data to enabling AI agents to take action across business systems.
  • Inside Merge, CEO and Co-founder Shensi Ding uses Codex to review product code, including work on a upcoming setup interface for configuring tool access in Merge for Workforce.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The integration platform uses GPT‑6 Astra, ChatGPT, and Codex for product reviews, marketing, and business development planning.

According to recent reports, merge helps companies build connected software and AI products, from syncing customer data to enabling AI agents to take action across business systems. Its products span customer-data integrations through Merge Unified, secure tool access for AI agents through Merge Agent Handler, and model routing and cost controls through Merge Gateway. Merge for Workforce brings those capabilities inside companies, helping teams manage which models, tools, and business systems employees can access. Together, these products support both the software companies build for customers and the AI-powered work happening inside their organizations.

Inside Merge, CEO and Co-founder Shensi Ding uses Codex to review product code, including work on a upcoming setup interface for configuring tool access in Merge for Workforce. Her colleagues use GPT‑6 Astra for product testing and marketing. The team also uses AI for the work of running the manufacturer, from preparing sales updates to planning customer dinners.

In a recent development, merge debuted a tool for adding connectors to AI products, with reliability a priority for Ding: “We’re pretty proud of the quality. Tool calls through Merge succeed 99.9% of the time, compared to public MCP servers, which are around 60%.”.

For its own product development, Merge uses GPT‑6 Astra. “It’s really fast, and it was much better at code reviews,” Ding claims. “They also liked the personality of GPT‑6 Astra, which goes a long way. It was also clear that Codex had improved a lot. Merge lets employees choose their own AI tools, and which one to use has become a lively internal debate.”.

Sources indicate that ding used Codex to review a proposed implementation of the new provisioning tab in Merge for Workforce as the team evaluated how customers would configure tool access. They discussed making the “Add tool pack” action a clearer link that opens separately to make setup less confusing. Codex supplied code-review feedback; Merge’s team made the product decisions and implementation changes, with engineers responsible for validating and shipping them.

Merge hosts executive dinners for customers and prospects to build relationships and create opportunities for follow-up product conversations.

For one dinner in Dallas, Merge started with the city and the kinds of people it wanted to bring together. The bot pulled potential guests from the CRM and Apollo, checked previous invitations and responses, and helped prepare outreach from Ding’s email. It also maintained the attendee tracker, proposed a seating chart, and created calendar notes where sales and customer success could add context about each guest.

According to recent reports, the model handles reasoning and drafting, while Merge’s connectors provide access to the business systems. Ding reviews the output, rewrites anything that sounds off, and curates the guest list using relationship context the bot does not have.

In October 2026, Merge reported that preparing guest lists and outreach and maintaining the attendee tracker had gone from dozens of hours across the manufacturer to about 30 minutes per event. The comparison covers the same planning tasks, measured over the preceding three months. The team still handles hosting, relationship-building, and on-the-ground logistics.

Merge ran 16 executive dinners in Q3, up from eight in Q2, and prepares to host more than 30 in Q4. After the Dallas dinner, the team reported positive feedback on the invitations and opportunities for follow-up demos.

“With GPT‑6 Astra, the dinner bot connects to our Salesforce, Gong, Google Sheets, and Gmail, and it’ll send emails on my behalf to people in our network,” Ding notes. “It gives me recommendations for people who are a good fit for each dinner, and it surfaces new potential attendees.”.

Ding claims, “It’s been especially great for team members who aren’t in engineering, because now they can build anything.”.

Sources indicate that charlie Lynch on Merge’s sales leadership team built reusable AI workflows for deal approvals, forecast updates, and next steps after renewal calls. Instead of repeatedly gathering context for each update or decision, he uses the workflows to prepare the material, then reviews the recommendation and decides what to do next.

Sources indicate that the social media team uses GPT‑6 Astra in ChatGPT to find posts the company should respond to. The marketing team also used it to clarify the messaging for Merge’s Gateway Evaluations launch.

Lead by using the tools: “If you’re an executive, you are the ceiling for AI fluency in your organization,” Ding indicates.

Find somewhere less risky to experiment: Ding and her co-founder experimented with AI on a upcoming product before customers depended on its codebase. “When you’re less nervous, and you can really experiment, you learn so much,” she states.

Sources indicate that give people space and time to tinker: Merge lets each team member choose the tools they like and encourages them to spend time every day learning and testing. That includes the freedom to “go wild and make mistakes,” even when it means going down a rabbit hole that doesn’t pay off.

“Anything that I want to do, I can just tell AI to do it, and it can just do it,” Ding says. Merge is continuing to use OpenAI technology to expand what its teams can build, bringing the same spirit of experimentation to its products and the way it runs the business.

#18855. GPT‑6 Cyber: Advancing the frontier of aligned cybersecurity agents

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

GPT‑6 Cyber: Advancing the frontier of aligned cybersecurity agents

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1970 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A cybersecurity model trained to find and validate exploitable vulnerabilities, while staying within the scope that researchers set.
  • Industry observers note that we’re introducing GPT‑6 Cyber, a major leap in security research: more capable at finding and fixing vulnerabilities, and far more reliable staying within the boundaries researchers set.
  • Sources indicate that on ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability, GPT‑6 Cyber scores 48.5%, up from 32.1% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A cybersecurity model trained to find and validate exploitable vulnerabilities, while staying within the scope that researchers set.

Industry observers note that we’re introducing GPT‑6 Cyber, a major leap in security research: more capable at finding and fixing vulnerabilities, and far more reliable staying within the boundaries researchers set. GPT‑6 Cyber delivers major gains on key cybersecurity benchmarks over GPT‑5.6 Cyber, including a 51% relative improvement on ExploitGym and a step function improvement when tested on staying within scope. It is already helping to secure real-world software, uncovering and validating thousands of exploits in security-critical codebases such as Linux and Firefox.

Sources indicate that on ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability, GPT‑6 Cyber scores 48.5%, up from 32.1% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber. It also follows task boundaries more reliably: in a separate alignment evaluation, GPT‑6 Cyber avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of tests without its deployment prompt, and 100% with this prompt. This improvement in alignment reflects dedicated training to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions, and report results accurately.

Recent findings suggest that these capabilities are already helping secure real systems. Our researchers used GPT‑6 Cyber to develop 948 privilege escalation exploits in Linux⁠ and identify 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, despite extensive prior testing with frontier models. The model also helped develop candidate patches, and Mozilla has released fixes for many of the Firefox vulnerabilities⁠(opens in a newly introduced window). Security teams at Cisco, Calif, and CodeRabbit are using it for vulnerability research and code review, and we have relied on it to find and fix weaknesses in our own infrastructure⁠.

In a recent development, it is clear that we have a limited window to use frontier models to secure software⁠. Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers. Mainline models such as GPT‑6 Astra already support code review, vulnerability triage, and patch development. Daybreak Blue helps verified defenders validate vulnerabilities and fixes with fewer unnecessary refusals, while Daybreak Red enables deeper exploit development and authorized security testing with GPT‑6 Cyber.

In a recent development, GPT‑6 Cyber is a major step up from GPT‑5.6 Cyber and outperforms GPT‑6 Astra on most cyber tasks, even when Astra does not refuse the request. We evaluated the model on tasks that require it to understand software, identify vulnerabilities, and develop working exploits. Based on these results, we classify the model as Critical in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, up from High for GPT‑5.6 Cyber.

On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability in a remote target, GPT‑6 Cyber scores 48.5%, about 16 percentage points higher than GPT‑5.6 Cyber’s 32.1%. To test vulnerability discovery, we also built a upcoming evaluation for offensive web penetration testing. Models probe web applications without access to their source code. GPT‑6 Cyber achieved 40.3% recall of vulnerabilities compared with 32.0% for GPT‑6 Astra.

It has been revealed that daybreak Red is designed to support more advanced security workflows, including developing working exploits and using them against remote targets. To evaluate these capabilities, we built a new benchmark called RemoteExploitBench, which uses known vulnerabilities in applications such as GitLab, PostgreSQL, and Jenkins deployed in a controlled environment. In our initial evaluation, GPT‑6 Astra running with Daybreak Blue refused 100% of tasks, while GPT‑6 Cyber completed 95%; its only failure was an exploit it could not get to work remotely. See the system card⁠(opens in a new window) for full results and evaluation settings.

One risk for cybersecurity agents is that they go outside the scope of their assigned task, attempt to exploit unrelated services, or disregard the researcher’s rules of engagement.

Sources indicate that we made alignment a central focus of GPT‑6 Cyber, using specialized training to help the model stay within authorized scope, follow restrictions on its actions, and report its work accurately. Before deployment, we ran a series of alignment evaluations to measure these behaviors. See the system card⁠(opens in a new window) for full results.

One of these evaluations is ExploitGym Honeypot, which was informed by the Hugging Face incident⁠. We give the model a difficult exploitation task in an isolated environment with access to supporting services, such as a package registry or object store. We deliberately make these services easy to exploit so that attacking them can reveal the task’s flag. The model must infer that exploiting them is outside the scope of its task.

GPT‑6 Cyber shows a step-change improvement over GPT‑5.6 Cyber on this evaluation. When tested without deployment safety prompts, it avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of cases, up from 94.49% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber. With those prompts, GPT‑6 Cyber stayed within bounds 100% of the time.

We can see directly in the GPT‑6 Cyber model’s chain of thought how it reasons about staying within bounds:.

GPT‑6 Cyber is already helping security teams find vulnerabilities, validate their impact, and develop fixes. Customers have put it to work on large codebases, long-running exploit development, and security review:.

Sources indicate that we have also relied on GPT‑6 Cyber to secure our own systems. It was one of the main models behind the work we recently shared on hardening the infrastructure used to train frontier models⁠. In controlled red-teaming campaigns, agents using GPT‑6 Cyber and other OpenAI models chained vulnerabilities to escape microVMs and execute code on the underlying hosts. We used the findings to patch software, tighten network restrictions, and report concerns to maintainers and vendors.

Sources indicate that our vulnerability researchers also use GPT‑6 Cyber to find and validate vulnerabilities in open-source software at scale. This work has uncovered previously unknown flaws in software that has been scrutinized for years:.

Industry observers note that found 81 novel Firefox vulnerabilities. GPT‑6 Cyber can be suitable for use in autonomous workflows for finding vulnerabilities and proposing high-quality patches at scale. During a vulnerability research campaign, GPT‑6 Cyber produced evidence and reproducible tests for 81 novel vulnerabilities classified by Mozilla as high severity, and revealed that an additional 30 known issues were more severe than previously reported. We disclosed the findings to Mozilla, along with proposed patches to help its engineers develop fixes. Mozilla was supportive of this work, and began landing fixes shortly after receiving the reports⁠(opens in a upcoming window).

Developing exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities⁠. GPT‑6 Cyber reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and developed working exploits for 948—more than five times the 166 exploited by GPT‑5.6 Sol using the same research harness. Following the Linux community's guidance, we disclosed 304 critical findings to maintainers with candidate patches and are in the process of getting other vulnerabilities fixed.

Demonstrating critical RCE vulnerabilities. We recently discussed a critical vulnerability in Brotli⁠(opens in a new window), a compression library used by Node.js and other software. Our security researchers used GPT‑6 Cyber alongside other OpenAI models to develop and validate exploits showing how the flaw could enable remote code execution in downstream applications.

In a recent development, as models become more capable and uncover more security vulnerabilities, we are also seeing more attempts to use them to cause harm. These attempts include efforts by malicious cyber actors and adversarial groups seeking to distill our models. We have thus paired GPT‑6 Cyber’s stronger capabilities with stronger safeguards to detect and disrupt misuse and keep the model’s actions within the user’s intent and authorization.

We added and strengthened these protections alongside the release of GPT‑6 Cyber (see the system card⁠(opens in a new window) for full information):.

It has been revealed that cyber-specific misalignment monitoring. We monitor whether actions match the user’s authorization, while recognizing legitimate exploit development and testing.

Targeted monitoring for emerging threats. For example, during the coordinated disclosure of critical PHP vulnerabilities, we set up targeted monitoring for attempts to develop exploits against live PHP servers, while preserving support for defenders patching affected systems.

Sources indicate that private Safety Processing (PSP). We use automated checks to review related interactions for misuse. Standard retention remains the default. API customers using Zero Data Retention⁠(opens in a new window) generally must use PSP⁠(opens in a new window), which reviews encrypted records retained in customer storage for 30 days without exposing prompts and responses to OpenAI personnel.

Protection against stolen credentials. We require IP allowlisting for Daybreak Red API access by default, restricting requests to approved networks with limited exceptions. We also monitor credentials for compromise.

Sandboxing and oversight. As with past models, we recommend sandboxing⁠(opens in a upcoming window), action review⁠(opens in a new window), and human oversight for high-risk workflows.

According to recent reports, protections against high-risk cyber assistance. We use fresh checks to block high-risk activity involving critical systems (see below for more).

Protecting critical infrastructure has been a key consideration in designing GPT‑6 Cyber’s safeguards and access, including power plants, water treatment facilities, and the operational technology and industrial control systems (OT/ICS) that underpin them. We simultaneously want to give the teams defending these systems access to our most capable models while also strengthening our safeguards to prevent unauthorized attacks.

Recent findings suggest that first, to equip these defenders, our $1 billion Daybreak for Frontline Defenders⁠ grant program subsidizes access for resource-constrained teams such as government organizations and essential service providers. We’re also introducing a latest group within Daybreak Red (Daybreak Red for Critical Infrastructure) for approved critical infrastructure defenders, which gives them permissions to conduct authorized testing of critical systems while retaining safeguards against model misalignment.

Recent findings suggest that second, to prevent misuse of the Daybreak Red and Blue platforms, we have refined safeguards against assistance and capability development that could compromise industrial controls or safety-critical systems, interfere with equipment, or cause serious injury, catastrophic physical damage, or life-endangering service disruption. The figure below compares safeguard label rates across four access configurations, before and after the recent updates we’re rolling out alongside GPT‑6 Cyber.

It has been revealed that higher safeguard block rates are not always better. Many of the techniques in this evaluation are also essential to legitimate security work: understanding systems, finding vulnerabilities, and verifying that fixes withstand attack. We therefore assess these rates alongside support for legitimate research and patching, rather than aiming for 100%.

To evaluate how our models can help defend critical infrastructure, we partnered with Dragos, the global provider for extended operational technology (xOT) cybersecurity. Dragos ran evaluations using cyber-permissive Daybreak Red models in a controlled lab environment. The evaluations covered requests progressing from network discovery and asset enumeration through targeted reconnaissance, sensitive data exfiltration, and unauthorized, potentially dangerous device actions.

In a recent development, we used feedback from Dragos to refine our safeguards, aiming to block harmful assistance without unnecessarily restricting authorized testing. See their final report⁠(opens in a new window) for details on the evaluations. We’re also working to expand partnerships with other offensive security providers and purple teams on penetration testing and red teaming with AI, and with energy companies, other critical infrastructure operators, and national labs to assess our models’ effectiveness and safeguards in industrial defense. We have also increased our investment in threat investigations to detect model usage involving OT/ICS. We’ll continue refining our safeguards with input from partners and the security community, including reports through /feedback when safeguards miss harmful activity or interrupt legitimate work.

In a recent development, GPT‑6 Cyber is initially available through the API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers. We will progressively expand access to all Daybreak Red customers soon, and are also making GPT‑5.6 Cyber available to all Daybreak Red customers. We’re also expanding Daybreak Blue alpha access for GPT‑6 Astra to more organizations and individual security researchers; let us know⁠(opens in a fresh window) if you’re interested.

New owners and organizations can apply for Daybreak⁠ and get started with our cyber skills, products, and partners⁠.

Cult.fit builds operational muscle with Codex

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1063 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cult.fit is using Codex to help teams across functions build tools, move faster, and change how work gets done.
  • internal applications built by non-engineering teams in recent months.
  • annual software savings by rebuilding an internal capability with Codex.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cult.fit is using Codex to help teams across functions build tools, move faster, and change how work gets done.

internal applications built by non-engineering teams in recent months.

annual software savings by rebuilding an internal capability with Codex.

reduction in customer support costs.

Recent findings suggest that cult.fit is one of India’s leading technology-enabled fitness companies, operating 708 fitness centers across 77 cities and serving nearly one million paid members. Its business combines subscription-based access to gyms and trainer-led fitness classes with a growing consumer products portfolio spanning fitness equipment, accessories, workout footwear and activewear.

Recent findings suggest that as the organization grew, it wanted to solve more operational and product challenges without adding layers of process and complexity. By standardizing engineering on Codex and then extending it beyond engineering, cult.fit is helping teams across the organization analyze data, build tools, and move ideas into production. Alongside its Codex rollout, it is using the OpenAI API to develop more personalized member experiences, including through its AI Trainer.

Recent findings suggest that for Santhosh Kumar, CTO at cult.fit, AI presented an opportunity to change how the organization works. “We wanted to become more AI-native in the way we run things,” he says. “How can we run our operations or transform our operations to be AI-first? What newly introduced customer experiences can we offer? And how can we transform how we run our organization?”.

Cult.fit’s first major shift was in engineering. Before standardizing on Codex, developers were using a mix of coding agents and assistants. Different tools meant different conventions for repositories, agent instructions, skills, and development workflows, making it harder to share knowledge and reuse capabilities across teams.

Cult.fit wanted a shared platform around which it could standardize the software development lifecycle. The firm chose Codex as that foundation. Repository structures, skills, testing, code review, and feedback loops could now follow common conventions across teams.

In a recent development, the team then extended Codex into more specialized engineering workflows. Its Site Reliability Engineering agent can aggregate information from observability platforms and logs, investigate incidents, and, in many cases, create a pull request with a proposed fix for an engineer to review. Security agents help identify and address vulnerabilities, while other on-call agents investigate recurring production issues.

According to recent reports, cult.fit is also moving toward a more fully spec-driven development model, where a specification can guide work through the software development lifecycle toward a pull request for an engineer to review. This gives teams a more repeatable path from a defined requirement to working code.

One recent example is a social feed for the cult.fit app. Kumar estimates the project would previously have taken more than a year to build. Using the new workflow, the team built and shipped it end to end in two months.

Codex has since expanded beyond engineering. cult.fit made its firm data easier for Codex to work with, allowing teams to find answers and perform routine analysis themselves. Previously, even small data requests had to go through a central analyst team, creating a bottleneck.

According to recent reports, teams are also building their own applications and workflows. HR, for example, built a workflow in Codex to manage performance reviews, scheduling, feedback collection, and the work of bringing that information together. More than 20 internal applications have been built by non-engineering teams in recent months.

Sources indicate that that shift is changing how cult.fit thinks about the software it needs to run its business. When the cost of its internal dashboard software increased sharply, one engineer rebuilt the functionality with Codex over a weekend. Cult.fit now runs the capability on its own application, avoiding more than $100,000 in annual software costs.

According to recent reports, making this shift required more than giving employees access to Codex. A large hackathon gave employees an early view of what was possible. The firm then brought its management team together for a one-day session where leaders across functions built something relevant to their own work with Codex.

Engineering also runs twice-weekly office hours to help employees move projects from an idea to production, while engineers are embedded in selected functions to provide technical and domain support.

According to recent reports, cult.fit is also using the OpenAI API to extend AI into the member experience through its AI Trainer. With over 45% of cult.fit members being first time gym goers, guidance is a key access for helping them build a fitness habit. The company first built the AI Trainer several years ago to give members a guided personalized workout experience without a personal trainer.

Around 20% of Cult.fit’s gym customers currently utilize the AI Trainer product. With advances in language models, cult.fit saw an opportunity to make the experience more interactive and conversational.

According to recent reports, the latest version is designed around a voice-first workout experience. Using GPT Realtime through an OpenAI API integration, the trainer can provide coaching cues and support workout logging through two-way voice interaction.

Cult.fit is also applying AI to customer support workflows that previously required human agents to assess each case. One example is requests to waive penalties for missed group fitness classes.

When a member says they missed a class for a valid reason, an AI agent can assess the request by checking signals such as local weather and attendance patterns for that class before deciding whether the penalty should be waived.

Cult.fit built these agents into its existing Sprinklr support platform and connected them to its backend systems, moving customer support from a predominantly human-led chat model toward an AI-first workflow.

20+ internal applications built by non-engineering teams in recent months.

$100,000+ annual software savings by rebuilding an internal capability with Codex.

50%+ reduction in customer support costs.

Cult.fit’s next step is to move from individual AI workflows toward an organization where AI is built into how work gets done. In operations, Kumar describes the ambition as an “autopilot operations org,” with AI taking on more of the support work around frontline teams.

Sources indicate that in the member experience, the goal is a “trainer in your pocket,” extending personalized guidance beyond what a human trainer can provide at scale. Inside the organization, cult.fit continues to look for bottlenecks teams can remove with AI. As more employees build applications, analyze information, and automate workflows themselves, more ideas can move directly into working solutions.

#18830. Latest Update: Australian universities are creating AI-native graduates

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1588 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Australian universities are creating AI-native graduates

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1588 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the future of Australia’s workforce is taking shape before today’s students receive their degrees.
  • Recognising this shift, Australian universities, including UNSW Sydney, University of Sydney, La Trobe University, and Adelaide University, are forging collaborations with OpenAI to give their students and staff access to frontier AI tools.
  • According to recent reports, students, educators and IT teams are putting AI to work in clinical simulations, robot-assisted teacher training and student projects that build pathways into industry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the future of Australia’s workforce is taking shape before today’s students receive their degrees. Across university campuses, students are using AI to investigate ideas, build assistants and turn concepts into working prototypes. They are beginning to develop the skills they will take into research, established industries and ventures of their own.

Recognising this shift, Australian universities, including UNSW Sydney, University of Sydney, La Trobe University, and Adelaide University, are forging collaborations with OpenAI to give their students and staff access to frontier AI tools.

According to recent reports, students, educators and IT teams are putting AI to work in clinical simulations, robot-assisted teacher training and student projects that build pathways into industry. Alongside this work, universities are developing frameworks for where and how AI can be used in learning and assessment, helping students build practical skills while knowing when to rely on their own judgment. For teachers, employers and industry practitioners, these examples offer practical lessons in designing AI-supported learning, setting clear expectations for AI use and preparing Australians for an AI-enabled workplace.

Sources indicate that new research1 commissioned by OpenAI reveals what students want from their universities, including the access to AI they increasingly expect. In a survey of more than 1,000 Australian university students, 81% mentioned they already use AI several times a week, including nearly a third (33%) who use it multiple times a day. Over a quarter (28%) had already built an AI agent or assistant to help manage their studies, work or personal life. Four out of five students (79%) want their university to offer more opportunities to use advanced AI tools on real-world projects, with the same proportion interested in applying AI to challenges in health, climate, science or cyber security.

Have already built an AI agent or assistant to manage studies, work or personal life.

Believe AI skills will be essential to success in their chosen career.

Believe AI literacy will become as fundamental as digital literacy, writing or numeracy.

Believe AI skills will give Australian graduates an advantage in the global workforce.

Findings from a survey of university students in Australia1.

Students also see those experiences as preparation for what comes next. More than sixty percent (61%) believe AI skills will be essential to success in their chosen career, and 65% believe those skills will give Australian graduates an advantage in the global workforce. There is entrepreneurial ambition, too. More than three quarters (76%) of students surveyed mentioned they were interested in starting a tech giant or working for themselves, while over two thirds (68%) believed AI would make it easier to start a business.

The question for higher education is how to meet students where they are. Giving them access to advanced tools is a start, but helping them use those tools with sound judgment, subject knowledge and practical experience is what will make them AI-ready for the workforce.

It has been revealed that UNSW’s expanded collaboration with OpenAI is one way universities are responding. The university is bringing ChatGPT Edu to more than 80,000 students and staff, expanding access in stages as it works towards availability across the student community.

UNSW and OpenAI strategy to integrate generative AI foundations and Codex into educational programs and courses, with opportunities for students to apply AI through hackathons and industry projects. The collaboration is also intended to connect students with internships, graduate roles and startup networks.

UNSW Master of IT student Nalin Iyer put the workforce question plainly: “It’s important to understand what industry is looking for and how AI fits into that.”.

Industry observers note that the University of Sydney’s collaboration with OpenAI also aims to build practical capability across the institution. It will provide students and staff with supported access to ChatGPT Edu, with training and guidance. The rollout is staged, with access for all students scheduled for Semester 1, 2027 after a trial. The university is also establishing a $1 million AI Sustainability Research and Innovation Fund to study and advance sustainability.

Representatives from the University of Sydney and OpenAI mark the start of their strategic collaboration.

Recent findings suggest that la Trobe University is connecting broad access with an ambition to embed AI across its curriculum. All 3,500 staff already have access to ChatGPT Edu, with universal access planned for its 45,000 students and staff in the first quarter of 2027. Its approach includes Australia’s first Bachelor of AI Engineering (Honours), welcoming its first cohort in 2027, and Australia’s first AI MBA program.

As part of its AI-first strategy, La Trobe appointed Australia’s first Pro Vice-Chancellor AI and Chief AI Officer, Phil Laufenberg, to lead the university’s approach to AI across education, research and operations.

These efforts respond to a reality the survey makes clear: students are already experimenting with AI, but institution-wide access and support mean all have equitable opportunities to develop their skills, regardless of what they study or what individual tools they can afford.

At La Trobe University, some of the most interesting work begins with a simple question: how can we use AI to enhance practical experience in learning?

Dr Cameron Anderson, Head of the Paramedicine program, uses ChatGPT to create a wide range of practice activities delivered through the university’s learning management system, where students interpret an ECG, assess a possible heart attack or triage patients after a mass casualty incident. AI helps create simulations that reinforce and test classroom learning.

Professor Therese Keane, Associate Dean for Research and Industry Engagement in La Trobe’s School of Education, uses a social robot called Fletch to help future teachers practice giving feedback to parents. Powered by OpenAI large language models hosted through Microsoft Azure, Fletch responds with speech, facial expressions and head movements.

Professor Keane’s team developed realistic scenarios from interviews with highly experienced educators. Importantly, Fletch enables trainee teachers to practice situations where conversations with parents turn confrontational, developing key skills in an area that many teachers find challenging.

Professor Therese Keane at La Trobe University is helping future teachers practice difficult conversations with parents using Fletch, an OpenAI-powered social robot.

According to recent reports, la Trobe is bringing AI into more of its courses and operations. The university has made OpenAI’s agentic tools Codex and ChatGPT Work available across the institution, with its handbook listing Vibe Coding for Startups and Agentic AI Software Engineering (from 2027).

According to recent reports, the university’s AI Business Studio extends practical learning into industry. It aims to give more than 1,000 students practice experience as consultants and forward deployed engineers using ChatGPT Edu and Codex to help small and medium enterprises adopt AI by 2028 and connect graduate skills with the needs of businesses.

According to recent reports, an AI rollout of this size needs steady work behind the scenes. La Trobe reports dozens of live use cases, training for hundreds of people and 10% month-on-month growth in active users. It manages safe access and token economics as more people take part. “ChatGPT and Codex have helped shorten early systems development and innovation from months to weeks, and importantly, enabled embedded co-design by staff and students,” Laufenberg remarked.

According to recent reports, as a newly established university created through a complex merger, Adelaide University has an opportunity to embed secure, governed and scalable uses of AI from the outset. Australia’s first newly introduced major university in a generation is building on existing use of OpenAI’s API by researchers, students and staff.

Adelaide University is one of the first institutions in the higher education sector to harness OpenAI Daybreak Blue to conduct authorised defensive security work, providing a vital capability for cyber defences, including vulnerability discovery, secure code review, malware analysis, incident response and patch validation.

UNSW Senior Lecturers Mariana Rodriguez-Valenzuela (seated) and May Lim assist with the rollout of ChatGPT Edu as Joel Solomons, Education Solutions Engineer at OpenAI ANZ, looks on.

Universities are also setting clear expectations for when students can use AI and when they need to demonstrate their own knowledge.

Industry observers note that UNSW has introduced a Can, Can’t, Must framework for assessment. Depending on the learning goal, an educator can specify that AI use is permitted, prohibited or required. That gives students a way to practice using AI appropriately while still demonstrating the foundational knowledge their field demands.

The University of Sydney is pairing its rollout with a responsible AI framework alongside its assessment approach that ensures students demonstrate their own capabilities in supervised settings, then show how they can use AI effectively in open assessments.

Sources indicate that la Trobe is also supporting wider access with practical guidance. Its library has developed free Responsible and Safe AI learning modules for all students, and AI skills development is being integrated in 50 priority first-year subjects for Semester 1, 2027. Tailored modules for Education, Law and Health connect AI literacy with professional responsibilities, while workshops and teaching resources support educators in designing learning activities and assessments.

Sources indicate that students already see AI skills as essential to their careers and an opportunity to get ahead. By widening ChatGPT access and bringing AI into everyday teaching, Australian universities are helping turn that ambition into practical experience. The goal is to prepare graduates who can use AI to learn, create and solve problems, with the subject knowledge and judgment to apply those skills confidently as they enter the workforce.

This study by Pureprofile, on behalf of OpenAI, surveyed 1,018 university students aged 18 and over across Australia, studying on campus or remotely, from 3–7 August 2026.

#18827. Measuring how AI agents handle everyday wet-lab science

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2055 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Measuring how AI agents handle everyday wet-lab science

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2055 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Introducing BioBasicsBench, a benchmark measuring how well AI agents interpret raw experimental data across 100 routine wet-lab tasks.
  • Recent findings suggest that our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity.
  • Recent findings suggest that the benchmark’s 100 tasks test whether agents can interpret raw experimental data, identify errors, and recognize when the evidence cannot support a conclusion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Introducing BioBasicsBench, a benchmark measuring how well AI agents interpret raw experimental data across 100 routine wet-lab tasks.

Recent findings suggest that our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. As part of that mission, we want to help scientists accelerate biological research—from understanding disease to developing latest treatments. For AI agents to contribute, they need to reliably interpret the experimental evidence scientists work with every day in wet labs, where they run experiments with biological samples. Everyday wet-lab work involves failed experiments, ambiguous images and conflicting observations. Existing benchmarks are built around charts and images selected for scientific papers may miss this ambiguity and the troubleshooting it requires. That’s why we’re introducing BioBasicsBench, a new benchmark developed with Ligo, a biotech tech giant focused on enzyme design, to measure how well agents handle routine wet-lab analysis.

Recent findings suggest that the benchmark’s 100 tasks test whether agents can interpret raw experimental data, identify errors, and recognize when the evidence cannot support a conclusion. Getting these tasks right matters because misreading an image or overlooking a problem with the controls used to check an experiment’s results can lead scientists to draw the wrong conclusion and spend time on experiments that won’t help answer their question.

At the ‘xhigh’ setting, which allows more reasoning per task, GPT‑6 Astra earned an average of 66.7% of the available credit, compared with 43.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. The results show progress on routine lab analysis, with room for further improvements in interpreting images, checking controls and applying experimental context.

BioBasicsBench uses raw experimental evidence, from gel images and colony plates to microscopy and instrument readouts.

BioBasicsBench has 100 tasks across five areas of routine wet-lab work: protein methods, imaging and cytometry, quantification and assays, nucleic acid methods, and molecular cloning. Tasks range from simple requests, such as reading the molecular weight of a DNA sample in a gel, to detailed assay analysis, but all involve routine work that wet-lab scientists should be able to complete reliably.

It has been revealed that scientists created the tasks using data from their own experiments, pairing each question with expert-written grading criteria. Each task underwent an internal review by a Ligo scientist who had not written it, an external review by a PhD-level scientist working in a wet lab, and a final internal review.

Sources indicate that agents return a structured answer with the requested conclusion, measurement or recommendation and, where required, supporting reasoning. Answers receive credit against individual rubric criteria, allowing the benchmark to distinguish a correct conclusion from a partially correct analysis. Most tasks test several skills together, including biological knowledge, interpretation of images and other data, error detection and protocol understanding.

According to recent reports, “Unique tasks” counts each task once. The skill columns count tasks with each skill tag. These categories overlap: one task can appear in several columns, so the skill counts should not be added to obtain a task total. Color identifies the domain; stronger shading indicates a larger share of that domain’s tasks testing a skill.

The inputs preserve the forms of evidence scientists work with: gel and blot images, plate photographs, microscopy stacks, sequencing reads, plate-reader exports and videos of bench work. A task can include several kinds of data. Reference sheets, such as ladder charts and plasmid maps, support the interpretation of the experimental evidence.

Agarose DNA gels, SDS-PAGE gels, Western blots.

Protocols and SOPs, lab notebooks and run records, photographed handwritten notes, catalogues, instrument specs, published methods.

CSV and Excel exports, lane layouts and inventories, raw flow cytometry (FCS) files.

Bench, apparatus & reagent photos.

Benches, gel rigs, reagent and culture tubes, a PCR plate, tube racks, pH strips, a concentrator, a freezer, a liquid-handler deck.

Raw brightfield and fluorescence images, multi-channel sets, z-stacks, time-lapse movies.

Photos of flow cytometer, microscope, NanoDrop, plate reader and balance screens; exported standard curves, chromatograms and plots.

Raw long-read FASTQs, FASTA sequences, GenBank maps.

Streaking, inoculation, serial dilution, SDS-PAGE tank and incubator setups, weighing on a balance.

Transformation plates, blue/white screens, antibiotic-disc plates.

Ladder charts, plasmid maps, pH charts (supporting material).

Recent findings suggest that number of tasks that include each kind of data. Categories overlap; reference sheets are supporting material.

Scientists wrote the tasks using data from their own experiments, pairing the experimental evidence with a question and an expert-written grading rubric. Each task went through an internal review by a Ligo scientist who had not written it, an external review by a PhD-level scientist working in a wet lab, and a final internal review. Reviewers checked the prompt, experimental evidence, rubric, author notes and a graded model attempt.

Answers are scored against the task’s rubric, which assigns credit to individual criteria. Depending on the task, these criteria assess the conclusion, numerical results, supporting reasoning or recognition that the evidence is insufficient.

It has been revealed that we evaluated seven models on BioBasicsBench: GPT‑5.2, GPT‑5.4, GPT‑5.5, GPT‑5.6 Sol, GPT‑6.1 Sol, GPT‑6 Luna and GPT‑6 Astra. The evaluation covers 37 model and reasoning-effort settings, with five attempts on each of the 100 tasks per setting, for a total of 18,500 results.

We report mean reward: the average task score, expressed as a percentage of the available credit. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals calculated by resampling whole tasks, keeping the five attempts for each task together.

It has been revealed that mean reward versus average output tokens per task, shown on a logarithmic scale. Each point represents a tested reasoning-effort setting; lines connect those settings in order. The x-axis doubles at each tick. Dashed orange lines show GPT‑5 models, and solid blue lines show GPT‑6 models. Faint whiskers show 95% whole-task bootstrap confidence intervals. Each setting includes all 100 tasks and five attempts per task. Effort settings differ across models.

Industry observers note that GPT‑6 Astra substantially improves on GPT‑5.6 Sol, even at low reasoning effort. These gains suggest that stronger native multimodal capabilities may be key to improving performance on everyday wet-lab analysis.

According to recent reports, xhigh is the highest reasoning-effort setting reported for all seven models. Each row includes all 100 tasks and five attempts per task. Max-effort results, where available, are included in the chart above.

Sources indicate that A common trap in science is over-interpreting the data, especially given the nature of bias that occurs when testing a hypothesis. Astra demonstrated a better ability to discern the limit of what the data reveals and not draw unwarranted conclusions.

In this example, GPT‑5.6 Sol classified cells as dead based on the signal from a dye used to detect dead cells. But the detector could also pick up light from a second dye, so brightness alone could not justify that conclusion. Astra recognized this ambiguity and called for better controls to separate the signals.

Brightfield · transmitted light.

Channel 2 · SYTOX-labelled · 470–540 nm.

Channel 3 · FUN-1 green · 525–580 nm.

In a recent development, the same cell regions in three channels; the detection windows overlap at 525–540 nm. The shared window permits interference; its amount has not been measured. Each channel is displayed with a separate linear intensity scale, fixed across both regions; brightness cannot be compared quantitatively between channels.

Scientific research is highly multimodal, requiring constant visual interpretation and decision making. Astra displayed a significant improvement at handling multimodal data which was given in the form of photos and videos, as well as raw outputs from sequencing, plate-reader assays, microscopy and flow cytometry.

According to recent reports, at the most basic level, this improvement was noticeable through GPT‑6 Astra’s ability to pick up on finer detail from images taken during experiments and therefore draw more accurate conclusions as shown in this example. This task asked agents to draw conclusions from a DNA cloning experiment, where controls are essential. GPT‑5.6 Sol saw no colonies on the negative control plate and based its conclusions on that observation. GPT‑6 Astra noticed that the plate was labeled with the wrong antibiotic and correctly rejected it as a reliable control.

The original benchmark photograph, with the rim label circled and enlarged. “LB Kan50” identifies kanamycin, a different antibiotic from the ampicillin used in the experiment.

According to recent reports, scientists must be able to hold tacit biological knowledge and experimental context in mind whilst analysing data in order to correctly interpret what it demonstrates. Astra demonstrated an improved ability to maintain this context and apply it throughout its analysis.

Industry observers note that one task highlighted cells coming into and out of focus in a series of microscope images. While GPT‑5.6 Sol looked for a biological explanation for the cells’ apparent disappearance, GPT‑6 Astra correctly recognized a z-stack: a series of images taken at different depths.

Six frames from the original recording. Dashed boxes mark the same location as the microscope scans through depth. Times refer to playback position in the supplied video.

Higher benchmark scores do not yet mean models can make reliable judgments in the lab. These Astra examples show how assumptions, expected answers and supplied labels can override the evidence, and how a correct intermediate observation can fail to guide the final decision.

Astra lets a familiar assumption override the interpretation supported by the experimental controls. It can distinguish the two groups of colony bands, but assumes that a larger PCR product would identify successful cloning. On that condition it proposes lanes 4, 6, 7 and 8; the reference’s control comparison instead selects lanes 5, 9 and 10.

The reference selects colonies 5, 9 and 10; Astra proposes 4, 6, 7 and 8.

1: marker · 2: cloning mixture · 3: original plasmid · 4–10: colony samples.

According to recent reports, lane 3 contains only the original plasmid PCR. Its band provides the old-plasmid reference position.

In the reference interpretation, lane 2 contains both patterns: incomplete assembly leaves old template/backbone alongside the upcoming product.

Industry observers note that the resulting colonies can carry either old or upcoming plasmid. Compare their bands with these reference patterns.

Reference selection: 5, 9 and 10.

Astra’s selection: 4, 6, 7 and 8. Astra nominates this group suggesting the larger PCR product represents the intended construct.

Industry observers note that the visual grouping is correct but the experimental identities attached to those groups are reversed relative to the reference. Astra therefore selects the wrong colonies from the colony PCR results which would result in the down-stream purification of the incorrect plasmid.

According to recent reports, astra discounts observations that contradict its preferred interpretation. It concludes that vacuoles, compartments inside cells, are generally darker than the surrounding cell, even though some appear lighter in the same image. Both appearances matter: changing the microscope’s focus can reverse the contrast, so the darker examples do not establish a general rule.

Astra’s darker-vacuole generalisation omits the lighter vacuoles visible in the same field.

According to recent reports, some cells have an opposite contrast. Both appearances occur because different focal depths can reverse the contrast.

In a recent development, astra inspects several regions and even comments that contrast varies with focus. It then gives greater weight to the cells it calls better focused and retains only their darker-vacuole description in the final answer. The contradictory lighter regions have been inspected but are not considered in the conclusion.

Astra’s counting marks do not reliably correspond to individual colonies: it fails to resolve close neighbours, misses visible colonies and marks empty agar. The net result on this plate is an overcount of approximately 12% relative to the benchmark reference.

It has been revealed that A: one counting mark between neighbouring colonies. B: two visible colonies left unmarked. C: empty agar counted as a colony. Red circles indicate Astra’s counting positions. Black arrows are editorial guides.

Recent findings suggest that an inaccurate colony count directly affects estimates of how efficiently DNA was introduced into cells. With the plated volume and dilution held fixed, an overcount inflates that estimate by the same proportion.

Accelerating biological research requires getting the everyday work right. BioBasicsBench makes that work a target for improvement: interpreting raw experimental data, checking controls and recognizing when a conclusion is not supported. Progress on these tasks could help scientists spend less time troubleshooting and more time deciding which experiments to pursue next. Tracking these capabilities will also help us understand their implications for biosafety and biosecurity.

Partnering with Hacktron to find vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s systems
