#18708. Tech Report: What’s upcoming in OKF v0.3: enterprise-ready knowledge, use cases, and skills

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1627 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Google ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: What’s upcoming in OKF v0.3: enterprise-ready knowledge, use cases, and skills

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1627 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In June we introduced the Open Knowledge Format (OKF), an open specification that provides plain markdown and YAML to give agents the context they need.
  • In production, bundles move between organizations, multiple agents edit the same corpus, and independent tools need to read a bundle the same way.
  • Sources indicate that we're also launching OKF use cases, which are community guides for using OKF alongside other industry standards, and two agent skills that let coding agents write and read OKF bundles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tech Lead, BigQuery, Engineering, Data Cloud.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

In June we introduced the Open Knowledge Format (OKF), an open specification that provides plain markdown and YAML to give agents the context they need. In July, v0.2 added trust signals: provenance, trust, freshness, lifecycle, and attestation.

In production, bundles move between organizations, multiple agents edit the same corpus, and independent tools need to read a bundle the same way. Released today, OKF v0.3 adds precise conformance rules, trust tiers that keep pace with agent edits, self-describing bundles with licensing, safe ways to retire and move knowledge, a stable extension model, and a clear versioning policy. However, the core idea behind OKF stays the same: type is still the only required field, and your existing bundles keep working.

Sources indicate that we're also launching OKF use cases, which are community guides for using OKF alongside other industry standards, and two agent skills that let coding agents write and read OKF bundles. Finally, to make cross-organization collaboration easier, we’re moving OKF out of the Google Cloud Platform GitHub org into a standalone organization at https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/.

Let’s take a closer look at what’s newly introduced in OKF v0.3.

v0.3 adds a formal conformance section, allowing independent producers and consumers to work together by design. The spec is self-contained and uses RFC 2119 keywords. It gives one clear answer to the questions that come up when tools from different teams and vendors read the same bundle. The full detail is in the spec, but a few themes matter for anyone building on OKF:.

Built on standard file formats. OKF uses a small, widely supported set of standards: YAML 1.2 frontmatter, CommonMark with GFM tables and footnotes, and RFC 3339 timestamps. If your tools handle those, they handle OKF.

Recent findings suggest that OKF bundles share space with other markdown files. A .md file without a type is skipped by OKF consumers, so README.md, AGENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, and SKILL.md can live inside a bundle without breaking it. Files that aren't markdown, like images or attester code, are assets that concepts can link to.

Consumers handle real-world input predictably. Bundles written by many agents can contain nulls, empty strings, single values where a list was expected, and upcoming vocabulary. v0.3 specifies how a consumer reads each of these. Consumers accept these inputs without failing, while validators log warnings for malformed entries. A bundle never fails because an optional field is missing or a link is broken.

v0.2 gave every concept a trust tier: unverified, machine-confirmed, or human-reviewed. As agents take on more of the editing, v0.3 makes sure the tier always reflects the latest version of the content. Here's a typical sequence:.

A person reviews a metric definition and signs off.

A week later, an agent refines the definition.

The trust tier now reflects that the person hasn't yet reviewed the new text.

Recent findings suggest that in v0.3, only current verifications count. A verification is current when it happened at or after the last meaningful change to the content, recorded in generated.at:.

This concept is now machine-confirmed, not human-reviewed, until a person confirms it again. The older sign-off stays in the file as history, and a UI can show it as "reviewed before the last change.".

In a recent development, v0.3 also standardizes actor identifiers. Actors are / for tools, or : for everything else, and v0.3 adds team: next to human: and process:. Only human: earns human-reviewed, because a team name doesn't say which person actually checked the content.

When an agent has access to dozens of bundles, bundle-level metadata supports progressive disclosure so it can pick the right bundle without reading every file. In v0.3, the bundle-root index.md can carry frontmatter about the bundle itself:.

Sources indicate that description is written for routing. In one sentence it indicates what the bundle covers and when to use it.

license makes clear what you're allowed to do with knowledge you receive from someone else.

okf_version tells a consumer which rules to apply, including compatibility fallbacks for older bundles.

Tools that regenerate index.md must keep this frontmatter.

According to recent reports, knowledge evolves, and an agent that finds a deprecated concept should be able to get to its replacement. v0.3 adds superseded_by:.

It has been revealed that consumers that filter to current knowledge follow the pointer and return the replacement. The same mechanism handles moves and renames. Leave a short deprecated concept at the old path that points to the upcoming one, and existing links and stored references keep working.

Links in the body and path fields in frontmatter (resource, superseded_by, executor.resource, and others) now resolve the same way:.

A value with a scheme (https:) is an absolute URL.

A value that starts with / resolves from the bundle root.

Anything else resolves from the directory of the file that contains it, just like on GitHub or in any markdown editor.

For bundles marked v0.2 or earlier, or with no version, a consumer can also resolve paths from the bundle root, so existing bundles keep working.

It has been revealed that v0.3 also makes explicit that links are not parent/child relationships. Only the directory tree defines hierarchy. A link is an untyped, directed relationship, and the text around it indicates what kind ("joins with," "replaces," "depends on"). Path fields that point at concepts are edges in the bundle graph too.

Sources indicate that the community has been extending OKF since v0.1, with typed edges, routing hints, and erasure profiles. v0.3 makes a few extension mechanisms a first-class rule:.

Extension keys are allowed at any level, including inside sources entries, verified events, executor, and attester.

A producer that edits a file must keep the keys it doesn't understand so one tool doesn't overwrite metadata added by another.

According to recent reports, future OKF versions will never define keys that start with x-. Name your keys x--, for example x-acme-owner, and they won't collide with a future spec version.

v0.3 defines OKF's versioning rules. Before 1.0, minor versions may include breaking changes as long as each is documented with a consumer fallback where possible. Starting at 1.0, minor versions will be strictly additive, and released normative text will not change in place.

Recent findings suggest that the spec also lists what was considered and deferred: typed relationships, the full attestation runtime protocol (receipt and verdict wire formats), semantic-layer attestation, validity windows, and a refuted verification event. Until the community agrees on a form for these, extension keys are the place to experiment. We'd like your proposals.

OKF keeps its core specification small and links to existing domain schemas like Avro, Protobuf, or OpenAPI instead of duplicating them. In practice, though, when your organization already has an established artifact in another standard, such as a schema, a contract, or a spec, what should the OKF concept next to it say, and how should an agent use the two together?

Starting with v0.3, we're publishing use cases: guides for using OKF with other industry standards. Each one explains:.

Where the boundary sits: what belongs in the other standard and what belongs in OKF.

How to link the two: which frontmatter and link conventions point from a concept into the other artifact.

What an agent should do with the combination.

A complete worked example you can copy.

According to recent reports, use cases are layered on the core spec, not part of it. A bundle that ignores them is still a conformant OKF bundle. When a convention proves itself across several use cases, it can be proposed for the core spec through the usual process.

Sources indicate that use cases are managed directly in GitHub. Each use case gets its own folder under usecases/ in the OKF repository, for example usecases//. The guide is a .md file in that folder, and any sample bundles or artifacts sit next to it. Use cases are reviewed, versioned, and discussed like any other change.

In a recent development, if you pair OKF with a standard, please send us a proposal. A rough first draft is welcome. Open a pull request that adds a folder under usecases/ with a .md file in it, and we'll refine it together in review.

v0.3 has two breaking changes, and existing v0.2 bundles stay readable:.

In a recent development, path fields resolve relative to their file. Fallback: for bundles marked v0.2 or earlier, or with no version, consumers can resolve from the bundle root.

Only current verifications count toward the trust tier. No fallback needed, since tiers can only go down.

It has been revealed that everything else is a clarification or an optional addition. v0.1 fallbacks (timestamp, body # Citations) still apply.

The two skills live in the latest repository and follow the open Agent Skills format, so any agent that supports skills can load them.

In a recent development, okf-generate writes, updates, migrates, and validates bundles from available sources. It cites a source for each claim, records a human review only when that person confirms it, and copies attested computations from a sanctioned source instead of writing them.

okf-consume answers questions from a bundle. For each concept used, it reports the trust tier, status, freshness, and attestation result, and runs attested computations only through the bundle's configured executor and attester.

To install them in Gemini CLI, run:.

The README lists the install steps for other agents.

Read the v0.3 spec. Add okf_version to your bundles, and check that your consumer computes trust tiers from current verifications only. Challenges and pull requests, including new use case proposals, are welcome on GitHub.

Spec, samples, use cases, and reference implementations: https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Introducing computer-use agents, improved clinical answers, and new healthcare plugins that work across healthcare software to get real work done.

Healthcare teams need to piece together information from the EHR, hospital policies, scheduling systems, and payer portals to deliver care and manage operations. With ChatGPT for Healthcare, we’re bringing the tools teams already use and the medical evidence they need into one platform to help them spend less time navigating systems and more time caring for patients.

It has been revealed that today, we’re sharing advances in computer-use agents⁠, which lets AI agents carry out multi-step work across existing healthcare software. We’re also improving trusted clinical search, which finds, evaluates, and cites medical evidence, and introducing more than 20 new plugins to the healthcare plugin ecosystem.

Together, these capabilities help healthcare teams find the information they need, make decisions grounded in medical evidence, and carry out next steps across the systems they already use.

Industry observers note that organizations often need to move information between disconnected systems to prepare documentation, coordinate care, and complete administrative tasks. Computer-use agents can help with these steps by navigating the software that teams already use: reading screens, clicking, typing, and moving between applications.

Today, we’re sharing advances in computer-use agents for healthcare, including more capable, safe, and affordable models for clinical and administrative workflows, and access controls and audit logs for secure deployments. We’re also sharing our work with healthcare organizations that are deploying agents, including Abridge, Ambience, Cigna Healthcare, and CVS Health, to process referrals, move documents between systems, and bring together the information care teams need. In the demo below, a clinician uses Voice in the ChatGPT app to ask for help following up on an MRI request. The agent reviews the chart and drafts an order and patient reply for review.

Healthcare organizations can start with a workflow that spans existing applications, set which applications agents can access, and establish clear controls for which steps require human review. To support HIPAA-compliant workflows involving protected health information, organizations must use eligible services covered by their BAA with OpenAI, apply required security and retention settings, and extend protections to connected systems. Content shared with ChatGPT for Healthcare is not used to train models.

Read more about our computer use research, customer stories, and demonstrations in Advancing computer-use agents for healthcare teams⁠.

We’re improving trusted clinical search in ChatGPT for Healthcare and ChatGPT for Clinicians, including how ChatGPT finds, evaluates, and cites medical evidence. These updates help clinicians connect relevant evidence to clinical questions and translate it into practical next steps, with citations they can inspect.

To measure the impact of these updates, in a blind evaluation, physicians reviewed responses to real-world clinical questions across multiple specialties, including multi-turn conversations. In over 1300 reviews, physicians rated the updated experience more highly across all eight dimensions evaluated, including factual correctness, safety, actionability, and source authoritativeness.

According to recent reports, we’re expanding our healthcare plugin ecosystem with more than 20 fresh healthcare plugins from leading companies across clinical care, care coordination, and business operations. All of these are available today in ChatGPT for Healthcare, including through ChartGPT, which brings ChatGPT into the EHR workflow⁠.

These plugins let teams bring more of their work into the same conversation: reviewing patient records and hospital protocols, preparing prescriptions for clinician review, coordinating patient outreach, checking insurance eligibility, and analyzing healthcare costs and operational performance.

See how healthcare teams can use these plugins together in ChatGPT.

ChatGPT for Clinicians is free for eligible, verified clinicians in the U.S. to review medical evidence and prepare clinical documentation. #18701. Our first phase of embedded assessments

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1820 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Our first phase of embedded assessments

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1820 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, we have signed agreements with four independent assessors—Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire—for our first phase of embedded assessments.
  • Embedded assessments give independent experts deep access to a lab’s internal models and systems to assess model alignment and the effectiveness of safeguards over an extended period of time, especially where relevant to our safety cases.
  • In a recent development, our initial assessments focus on alignment and safeguards for models during training and internal use, complementing our safety cases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we have signed agreements with four independent assessors—Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire—for our first phase of embedded assessments. As AI capabilities advance rapidly and the potential risks grow, public reporting from independent assessments can give people a clearer view of how labs are evaluating and managing those risks.

Embedded assessments give independent experts deep access to a lab’s internal models and systems to assess model alignment and the effectiveness of safeguards over an extended period of time, especially where relevant to our safety cases. Based on what each evaluation needs, assessors receive access to some of the same internal resources our researchers use, including model checkpoints, source code, training and evaluation data, monitoring systems, technical documentation, and discussions with the researchers and engineers responsible for the work. This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated.

In a recent development, our initial assessments focus on alignment and safeguards for models during training and internal use, complementing our safety cases. They build on our priorities and principles for third party assessments and years of work with third party evaluators, including a recent pilot assessment of our internal monitoring systems⁠(opens in a latest window) with deep internal access and an investigation of the Hugging Face incident⁠(opens in a new window). We’ll use what we learn to deepen our work with independent experts in the coming months. These efforts also support our commitments under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, where we agreed to independent assessments of our safety controls. These collaborations can contribute to stronger shared standards for independent assessment and public transparency across the industry.

Recent findings suggest that in this pilot assessment, Apollo Research⁠(opens in a new window) will assess whether models could covertly work against their developers’ intentions and whether our safeguards would detect such behavior. Drawing on evidence from training, safety testing, and internal use. Apollo will assess four claims in two stages:.

Training did not incentivize subversion.

Strong evaluations and red teaming do not elicit subversion.

Models have not attempted subversion during internal use.

Reasoning behind subversion would be detectable.

For the first stage of Apollo’s assessment, we’ll provide access to selected public and unreleased models and training checkpoints, relevant training data and evaluation results, training intervention records, monitoring systems and flagged behaviors, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.

It has been revealed that goodfire⁠(opens in a latest window) will embed interpretability researchers and use the Goodfire platform to analyze model internals. The main objective of their assessment is training run monitoring, debugging, and alignment. The primary audience for their assessments are internal OpenAI researchers, who will use their findings to make safety improvements. Goodfire will also publish learnings and findings as the collaboration progresses.

We intend to conduct two assessments with METR⁠(opens in a latest window), focused on model alignment and monitoring:.

Alignment assessment: For the first phase, METR will assess misaligned behavior in our largest reinforcement learning run to date, including failures that our existing tests and monitors may have missed. Within the selected run and agreed access, resources, and safety arrangements, METR would independently set assessment priorities and iterate on searches, analyses, and elicitation experiments. Access will include sampling relevant checkpoints, training and eval rollouts, and misalignment monitoring records for this run. For this first phase, the assessment will focus on our largest frontier RL run.1.

Monitor assessment: We recently worked with METR to conduct a monitor stress testing exercise2. We have preliminarily agreed to conduct another monitor assessment⁠(opens in a latest window) which we intend to be broader, but this is pending mutual agreement on the assessment scope.

Transluce⁠(opens in a new window) will conduct an initial assessment of our post-training alignment evaluations, examining their quality and coverage. For the initial assessment, we will provide Transluce with access to selected public and unreleased models, our post-training alignment evaluations and relevant results, supporting model behavior data and safety case documentation, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.

OpenAI and Transluce also share the intent to conduct a follow-on assessment of approximately eight weeks in early 2027, with broader access to additional models, deeper access to our alignment evaluations, and information on how evaluation results inform model release decisions.

We’ve developed protocols and processes with input from the assessors to balance deep access with security, confidentiality, oversight, and the independence and integrity of assessments. We are sharing them to shed light on how we will work with embedded assessors, and to advance discussion about norms for embedded assessments, which have yet to be standardized. We expect that these will need to evolve as we learn more about how to best conduct these assessments. Especially in the early stages of embedded assessments, we expect technical access challenges, space constraints, evolving security protocols, and other unexpected problems to arise. We hope to work through these challenges collaboratively with our embedded assessors and share lessons learned.

In a recent development, each engagement begins with an agreed scope and the access, resources, and safety arrangements needed to conduct a rigorous assessment. Some assessments test specific safety claims; others give assessors room to discover unexpected failure modes within a defined system or training run. In both cases, assessors need the freedom to follow evidence, refine their methods, and propose further assessments when findings warrant it. We also have a process for addressing additional access needs as assessments develop. When direct access could expose our most sensitive IP, such as model weights or architecture, we will consider alternatives, including pairing assessors with OpenAI researchers to run analyses.

Assessors who need access to sensitive confidential information will work on site at OpenAI offices and be provided OpenAI devices to conduct their work. The primary purpose is to protect the security of the information they access. Working onsite also gives assessors the opportunity to engage with dedicated staff who can help them navigate their access and provide context for their assessments. We also expect our embedded assessors to follow at minimum3 the same security standards as OpenAI employees when running experiments and evaluations.

Our Safety and Security Committee (SSC), an independent oversight committee of the OpenAI Foundation’s Board, will have visibility into the embedded assessment and the ability to exercise their oversight responsibilities before, during, and at their conclusion. They will receive unredacted reports, and both the assessors and the SSC will be able to speak with each other during the assessment, including privately. Disagreements among OpenAI and any evaluator will be escalated to the Safety Advisory Group and OpenAI executives, who will have a specified time period to resolve them, and the SSC will be notified of any such disagreements promptly when escalated. If a disagreement remains, the matter will be referred to the SSC for resolution.

Discussions with employees help assessors understand internal information and the context behind the work. OpenAI will authorize and provide guidance to staff members who can speak to assessors, and assessors may request additional staff to speak with as needed. To encourage open, candid conversations and protect the privacy of our staff, these discussions are off the record, meaning that they can inform the assessments but cannot be published or attributed to employees. Through a separate attestation pathway, assessors can request OpenAI-attested statements verifying, correcting, or clarifying something they learned in conversation with employees. These statements are not attributed to individuals or intended to characterize individual views. Assessors may publish statements that OpenAI attests to, or disclose that OpenAI declined to attest to a statement.

Recent findings suggest that managing conflicts of interest clearly and transparently—including those involving personal relationships, financial interests4, and other complications—is key to the integrity and independence of evaluations. Cool-off periods5 also need to be designed carefully, so assessors can work responsibly across labs while handling competitive information sensitively. We are working with our assessors to develop clear processes for both conflicts and cool-off periods, including allowing for flexibility in mitigations and transparency in decisions to request recusal.

Assessors maintain independence in publishing their assessments, but we will retain the right to redact confidential information, consistent with our previous third-party engagements. We may also request responsible disclosure delays to allow time to act on findings that could pose security or safety risks and remediate complications that remain.

Public reporting will help people understand the findings and their limitations, while more detailed confidential reports give oversight bodies the evidence they need to act. We want these assessments to improve how we identify and address risks, and give the public a clearer basis for judging our safety work.

These assessments bring an independent perspective to our ongoing alignment and safety work. Public reporting on their findings will make that work more transparent and provide greater assurance about how risks are being identified and addressed. We expect this first phase of assessments to lead to longer-term, consistent embedded engagements over time that can continuously provide third party safety signals and recommended improvements on our most load bearing safety claims and safety cases.

We’ll continue working with multiple independent third parties to help build a healthy assessment ecosystem with diverse expertise and approaches. Some investigations need sustained, on-site work with sensitive systems; others primarily evaluate deployed or soon to be deployed models or review public documentation.

In the coming months, we’ll support external assessments across a broader range of safety questions. We are also exploring future embedded assessments that would examine compliance with our safety frameworks, as well as our organizational culture and processes. We are committed to expanding this work and helping build the capacity and shared standards needed to sustain it.

This scope is less expansive than what METR outlines in their alignment assessment proposal⁠(opens in a new window), which envisions a broad survey of misalignment.

We recently conducted a 3 week long monitor red teaming exercise with METR, which granted them access to our codebase, monitors, relevant trajectories, and discussions with OpenAI research staff for the purpose of better understanding our monitors. https://metr.org/blog/2026-10-22-red-teaming-openai-agent-monitoring/⁠(opens in a upcoming window).

In some cases, there will be more stringent standards applied depending on the conditions of the experiment to allow for careful security vetting.

Apollo Research and Goodfire accept financial compensation for their work, but their compensation is not contingent on the results of their assessment. METR and Transluce do not accept financial compensation for their assessments, but may accept API credits / compute to use within their assessments. We do not believe that accepting financial compensation prevents assessors from maintaining independence - but we believe it is vital to disclose this.

We ask staff at third party organizations who participate in an embedded assessment to observe a brief cool-off period before embedding with another AI developer, to reduce the risk of inadvertent disclosure of confidential information.

#18700. Sashiko: Lessons from building an agentic code review system for Linux

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2126 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Google ↗ Open Full Page

Sashiko: Lessons from building an agentic code review system for Linux

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • VP, Infrastructure & Google Fellow, AI & Infrastructure.
  • Recent findings suggest that the speed of development in large open-source projects has always been limited by code review, not code generation.
  • According to recent reports, linux runs billions of Android phones, most cloud providers, and nearly every supercomputer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Software Engineer, AI & Infrastructure.

VP, Infrastructure & Google Fellow, AI & Infrastructure.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Recent findings suggest that the speed of development in large open-source projects has always been limited by code review, not code generation. Even as coding agents get better at writing code, they do not accelerate development on their own. This is especially true of patches to the Linux kernel. Without a way to build trust in proposed changes, more generated code simply piles up in front of the same small group of human maintainers. Some of those patches are solid changes, just written faster; many others are plausible-looking "AI slop" sent by contributors who do not fully understand the systems they are modifying. And the influx of AI-generated security reports, many of which are duplicates or inaccurate, only adds to maintainers’ load.

According to recent reports, linux runs billions of Android phones, most cloud providers, and nearly every supercomputer. It spans more than 35 million lines of code, and over 85,000 changes land every year. Automated build bots and fuzzers like Syzkaller catch build errors and crashes, but code review has always been the main way to guarantee the stability and safety of the kernel. Every day, maintainers read hundreds and hundreds of proposed patches by hand to catch memory leaks, deadlocks, race conditions, and security bugs.

To help maintainers handle the load and catch bugs before they land, the Google AI & Infrastructure team built Sashiko, an open-source, agentic code review system powered by Gemini. We named the project after the Japanese word 刺し子, a stitching technique for artistically reinforcing worn cloth, and donated it to the Linux Foundation earlier this year.

In this blog, we cover the problem Sashiko was designed to solve, how it works, what the data shows, and what we learned from building and running it in the wild.

Sources indicate that reviewing a change in a complex code base is objectively hard, both for humans and LLMs. It often requires a deep understanding of how the system works in general, well outside the proposed change. In fact, it’s pretty common to see patches that engineers claim perfectly solve the problem, but if they were to be merged, would actually introduce even worse problems (albeit subtle). Traditionally, only experienced maintainers have been able to spot and prevent these issues. The same is true for agentically generated code.

To verify the correctness of a change, a potentially large number of invariants should be proven, which is often a much larger and harder task than developing the change itself. This is true for both human and agentic reviewers. However, LLM-based reviewers have some unique properties, both positive and negative:.

To avoid these failure modes, Sashiko separates finding candidate bugs from verification of those bugs, and requires each pass to record what it ruled out:.

Gather context and initiative: Sashiko first pulls in the code around the diff (modified functions, struct definitions, and direct callers) and loads the subsystem's domain guides, so the changed lines are never judged in isolation. A planner then decides which specialist passes are needed (skipping hardware checks on pure software code, for example) and sets a reasoning budget for each pass based on patch complexity.

Parallel specialist sessions: Up to seven specialist sessions run in parallel, each focused on a single class of problems: commit intent, implementation match, control flow, resource lifetimes, locking, security, and hardware. Giving each pass a single focus prevents one type of bug from crowding out another. Each session searches and reads the repository with git tools (averaging about 100 tool calls per review) and outputs two lists: concerns it believes are real, and candidate concerns it investigated and ruled out, along with the code that supports that conclusion.

Triage: A lead verifier audits those two lists together. Clear-cut bugs already proven by the code in front of it pass straight through; dismissals proven by a local check are dropped. Everything else deserves additional investigation. Crucially, that includes not only contested bugs where specialists disagreed, but also shaky self-dismissals — cases where a specialist spotted a real bug and dismissed it by assuming, without proof, that some unseen caller or lock would prevent it.

According to recent reports, per-bug deep checks: Instead of checking all difficult cases in one shared prompt, Sashiko gives each difficult case its own verification agent that runs in parallel. Each agent gets one specific question to answer with git tools under a symmetrical rule: Neither a bug claim nor a dismissal is accepted without concrete code proof across all call sites. If a specialist talks itself out of a real bug based on a false assumption, this step catches it and promotes it back to a real finding.

Review report: Sashiko generates a report that sounds like a human maintainer asking questions about the proposed change, matching the style expected on a Linux mailing list.

Sources indicate that all this happens at no cost for developers. Deep agentic reviews at scale require a substantial token budget. If developers had to pay for them with their own API keys, many vital contributors would be pushed away. Instead, Sashiko reviews patches sent to public Linux kernel mailing lists, and Google runs the service at sashiko.dev. Everything runs in the open: every prompt, tool call, reasoning step, and ruled-out bug is public. The project initially used the open-source Linux review prompts started by Chris Mason, and more than 100 contributors, including prominent kernel maintainers and engineers, have since helped to improve prompts and Sashiko itself. Recently, Sashiko switched to a different prompt system that combines per-tree or per-version auto-generated notes on code with subjective maintainers notes, which contain directions and instructions from maintainers that can’t be derived from the code.

Industry observers note that the real test of an automated reviewer is whether maintainers pay attention to the reports it sends out, and whether those reports track actual software quality. Seven months of Sashiko production data from the kernel mailing lists give a clear picture of both these questions.

Industry observers note that it is part of the daily workflow. Sashiko completes roughly 1200 reviews a day across over 100 kernel mailing lists. It sends review emails only to lists whose maintainers opt in, and already over 70 of them have done so. Developers also engage directly with the reports: More than 1500 kernel developers have replied on the mailing lists, and their pushback on false alarms has directly driven improvements to Sashiko's prompts and verification engine. In fact, LWN.net recently wrote that Sashiko has already become an notable part of the kernel's development process and was the top bug reporter of problems in the 7.2 release cycle.

It prevents fresh bugs and uncovers old ones. When Sashiko flags a bug in a proposed patch, the author typically fixes it in the next revision before the change is ever merged. Many developers run Sashiko locally or in corporate private instances. The bugs that Sashiko helped to prevent leave no trace in the git commit log, making them hard to count directly. What can be counted are fixes for preexisting bugs that Sashiko finds and reports as a byproduct of reviewing new changes: Sashiko is cited in over 2000 mainline kernel commits and in over 500 of this year's official Linux kernel CVEs, spanning drivers, core kernel code, networking, GPUs, memory management, and virtualization.

Industry observers note that fewer bugs are slipping into mainline releases. Across the 18 kernel releases prior to Sashiko (Linux 6.2 through 6.19, covering 254000 commits), an average of 3.4% of merged commits required a follow-up fix within 60 days. Since Sashiko rolled out, that 60-day fix rate has fallen to 2.8% in Linux 7.1 and 2.2% in Linux 7.2, a 35% drop (with the 30-day fix rate falling from 2.3% to 1.4%). It’s too early to make strong claims, and obviously many other factors can influence release-to-release numbers, so we cannot solely credit Sashiko for the entire drop, but the trend is optimistic.

Sources indicate that A clean review carries real signal. If Sashiko's warnings were mostly noise, commits merged with warnings would need follow-up fixes no more often than commits that passed cleanly. In practice, across 21,500 tracked mainline commits, patches that received a clean Sashiko review required a follow-up fix within 60 days just 0.9% of the time — less than a third of the historical baseline. Patches merged despite a critical Sashiko warning needed a fix 7.6% of the time — an 8x higher risk (and 6.3x higher even after adjusting for patch size).

That gap is what makes Sashiko useful to maintainers: A clean pass instills real confidence, while a critical warning is a strong reason to take another look at the proposed patch.

This all tracks with what Linus Torvalds wrote in a mailing-list discussion a few weeks after Sashiko’s launch:.

Recent findings suggest that "As you say, Sashiko tends to be quite good. Even when it flags something unnecessarily and there's no actual problem, there's likely to be a reason for the question. And we've seen some truly stellar reports too. Things that are deep and subtle, and the AI is 100% correct. So anybody who thinks that all AI is slop is in denial about the current state." - Linus Torvalds (on lore.kernel.org).

Opted-in kernel subsystem lists.

Mainline commits crediting Sashiko.

2026 Linux kernel CVEs crediting Sashiko.

Down from 3.4% baseline to 2.2% (Linux 7.2).

First, benchmark-driven development beats intuition. While developing Sashiko, we tried many ideas that looked very reasonable on their face but didn’t end up working out. Other ideas were less obvious but worked surprisingly well. What was crucial: Early on, we built a benchmark out of nearly 1,000 real Linux kernel bugs and used it to evaluate every major Sashiko change. Every bug in this set was a real mistake that had passed human review by kernel experts, had been merged into mainline Linux, and later had to be fixed. On that benchmark, Sashiko with the newly introduced Gemini 4 Carbon model catches 75.8% of the bugs that human reviewers missed (using high thinking level).

According to recent reports, second, coding agents are not great at reviewing their own code. Models are trained to produce a working solution within a limited token budget. Asking these agents to review their own code might work well for isolated tasks, but for real, large codebases, creating a functional solution is often just 5-10% of the work. What’s really hard is to produce a solution that works all of the time, is well-integrated into the surrounding code, and doesn’t introduce subtle regressions. This is often substantially more complex and requires additional effort. Similar to human developers, agents benefit from external code review: Reviewers often spot complications that the initial author missed, even if they are not more experienced.

In a recent development, third, open source and shared community ownership and development help to build trust. By being fully open and transparent from the beginning, Sashiko allowed anyone to run it the way they wanted: using different models (including open source and local models), customizing prompts, or even adopting Sashiko to other-than-Linux projects. This helped with community adoption and brought over 100 contributors to improve Sashiko, including some prominent kernel developers.

More and more engineers are putting local Sashiko instances into their coding-agent loops, so patches are checked against the community's review rules before a human maintainer ever sees them. We use the same workflow to build Sashiko itself ("Sashiko for Sashiko"), running it to review every change to its codebase and prompt pipeline both locally and through a Github integration.

Although Sashiko started in the Linux kernel, the need for an agentic trust layer applies across critical open-source software. Because the core review engine does not depend on C or on kernel-specific rules, the Linux kernel playbook (combining an open verification pipeline, community-owned domain guides, and a benchmark mined from historically known challenges and fixes) can likely be applied to other foundational open-source projects such as GCC, LLVM, or Git.

Industry observers note that "Now, I think the other side of AI - and this is where Sashiko comes in - is that it basically does end up being a tool that can then increase the trust in the patch. So AI giveth, and AI taketh away. But the basic issue shouldn't be AI per se, it should be that notion of 'trust'." - Linus Torvalds on LKML.

You can check out Sashiko at sashiko.dev, or find the code on GitHub to run it in your own development workflow.

Paris, 16 November 2026—LVMH Group’s Media Division and OpenAI announce the signing of a strategic agreement to support newly introduced uses of artificial intelligence across all the division’s publications and make their journalism more accessible through ChatGPT. The agreement includes the deployment of OpenAI tools and ChatGPT Enterprise to teams across the media division, enabling them to develop AI applications tailored to their day-to-day work.

Their shared ambition is to empower teams across the media division to experiment with and develop practical uses of AI that support journalism and high-quality reporting.

Industry observers note that artificial intelligence is a powerful tool that, when put to work in newsrooms, enables journalists to focus on the core of their profession: investigating, analysing and writing. Teams will be able to explore applications such as document research, document comparison and preliminary translation. The goal is to enable them to devote more time to investigative reporting, analysis and reporting in the field.

Recent findings suggest that in addition, in an increasingly crowded information landscape, personalisation has become a major priority. Artificial intelligence is an essential tool for developing and delivering products and services that meet the needs of customers, readers and advertisers alike, helping to attract and retain them and grow revenue across the publications.

This partnership is a firm-wide initiative that also enhances the presence of content from LVMH Group’s Media Division in ChatGPT, providing summaries and excerpts in response to relevant user questions, identifying their sources and including direct links to the original articles. The partnership will extend across all the division’s publications and support the evolution of roles throughout the organisation: streamlining operations, improving efficiency, and encouraging innovation and creativity to prepare today’s publications for tomorrow. The rollout will be supported by training tailored to everyone’s use cases.

LVMH Group’s media division, Groupe Les Echos-Le Parisien, brings together 17 media brands covering news, finance, culture, heritage, arts and music. With 1,800 employees, including nearly 700 journalists, it reaches more than 27 million people in France every month.

The Group’s media brands: Boursier.com⁠(opens in a new window), Capital Finance, Challenges, Connaissance des Arts, Historia, Investir, La Lettre de l’Expansion, L’Agefi, Le Parisien, Aujourd’hui en France, Les Echos, L’Opinion, medici.tv⁠(opens in a new window), Mezzo, Mieux Vivre Votre Argent, Paris Match, Radio Classique.

The Group’s exhibitions and publishing houses: Citadelles & Mazenod, Fine Arts Paris, In Fine, Salon du Dessin.

VP, Global Startups & Investor Ecosystem.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

As thousands of founders, investors, and technology leaders gather in Helsinki for Slush 2026, the European startup ecosystem is undergoing a profound transformation. The conversation has moved from  AI experiments to operating agents. Across Europe, the Middle East, and Africa (EMEA), pioneering startups are deploying autonomous AI agents that reason, integrate deeply with core systems, and automate complex workflows at scale.

At Google Cloud and Google DeepMind we’re focused on delivering a complete AI stack for startups,including; Gemini Enterprise and the Gemini agent; the industry’s broadest choice of proprietary models including Gemini, Claude, GPT; open models like Gemma; multiple compute options including both GPUs and TPUs;  the infrastructure required to build and scale AI applications; and the tools to manage huge volumes of data, monitor token spend, and more.

This week at Slush, we are proud to highlight a remarkable group of European startups leveraging Google Cloud’s secure infrastructure and Gemini models to redefine their industries:.

According to recent reports, CDON (Sweden): As the largest e-commerce marketplace in the Nordics, CDON modernized its backend and data infrastructure on Google Cloud. Its analytics pipelines run on Google BigQuery, dbt, and Google Cloud Storage, utilizing Python and FastAPI to ingest massive volumes of retail marketplace data. CDON democratizes real-time business reporting across brands and lays the groundwork for predictive personalization and generative AI workloads.

Recent findings suggest that chalkie.ai (UK):  A fast-growing education technology platform, Chalkie.ai uses Gemini's advanced reasoning capabilities to transform lesson planning for over 500,000 educators. By exporting directly to Google Slides Google Slides, teachers can instantly generate curriculum-aligned presentations and materials directly within their instructional tools while maintaining strict student data privacy standards.

Sources indicate that finova (UK): A leader in UK lending and savings software, has launched the UK’s first whole-of-market AI mortgage application agent, built on Google Cloud and Gemini. By deploying Gemini’s advanced reasoning to automate complex mortgage applications across multiple lender portals, Finova removes manual data entry bottlenecks and reduces errors. This saves mortgage brokers at least 30 minutes per application and reclaims thousands of operational hours industry-wide.

Fyndiq (Sweden): Swedish e-commerce marketplace Fyndiq (part of CDON Group) anchors its predictive analytics and data operations in Google BigQuery, dbt, and Google Cloud Storage. Fyndiq models transaction and product feed data to deliver near real-time business insights to merchandisers. By applying Google’s machine learning and performance models, Fyndiq optimizes customer acquisition and regional campaign reach.

In a recent development, via Health Tech (Germany): Berlin-based VIA HealthTech is the AI assistant for psychotherapists. Powered by Gemini's multimodal audio and reasoning capabilities on Google Cloud, VIA turns therapy sessions into structured clinical notes within seconds and drafts psychological reports, giving therapists their time back for their patients. Trust is built in: VIA's security and compliance setup is BSI C5 attested and ISO 27001 certified, so therapists can use AI without compromising their professional secrecy. More than 4,000 clinicians already rely on it.

Building sustainable AI businesses requires infrastructure that combines high computational performance with strict data governance and predictable cost efficiency. This week we rolled out the Google for Startups Accelerator: Sovereign AI (Europe & Israel). This equity-free, 12-week hybrid program is tailored for late-Seed to Series A startups handling high-stakes, regulated workloads across sectors like GovTech, HealthTech, and financial services. Participating founders receive 1:1 architectural mentorship from Google Cloud engineers, technical advisory support to prepare for EU AI Act regulatory sandboxes, and hands-on guidance deploying across our tiered sovereign portfolio—from the Google Cloud Data Boundary and partner-operated clouds like S3NS to air-gapped Google Distributed Cloud environments and open-weight models like Gemma.

Additionally, through the Google for Startups Cloud Program, startups across EMEA receive up to $350,000 in cloud credits , dedicated engineering support, and preferred access to partner tools and our AI infrastructure and models.

Whether you are building agents, scaling multi-modal applications, or migrating to scalable cloud infrastructure, Google Cloud provides the foundation for the next generation of EMEA startups .

If you are attending Slush 2026 in Helsinki, visit the Google Cloud booth to meet our engineering and startup teams, explore interactive demos, and learn more about applying to the Google for Startups Cloud Program.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • With OpenAI models and Codex, Revolut is giving its teams more room to solve complex problems—from software engineering to financial crime.
  • Reduction in coding time from task start to feature merge.
  • To turn seven years of design documentation into AI-readable context.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With OpenAI models and Codex, Revolut is giving its teams more room to solve complex problems—from software engineering to financial crime.

Reduction in coding time from task start to feature merge.

To turn seven years of design documentation into AI-readable context.

Saved on security code review with Codex.

Revolut⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) was built to challenge the way people interact with money. That ambition now stretches across more than 40 markets, 800,000 businesses and a consumer base that’s grown by 23% in the last 12 months.

Add to that a organization culture that expects small, lean teams to move quickly and it’s no surprise that ChatGPT and Codex have proven a natural fit.

“The perfect description for a high-caliber Revolut person is someone who can identify a problem really quickly, deduce the solution, design four scenarios, identify the best one of those four then take it to market,” says Kim Maniovich, Revolut’s Global Head of Business Marketing.

“Partnering with OpenAI enables us to build a lot of these solutions in a way that’s incredibly lean, cost-efficient and really tailored to the unique way that we work.”.

Recent findings suggest that but moving faster is only part of the opportunity. For Revolut, the bigger question is what becomes possible when talented people spend less time on the mechanics of getting things done—and more time tackling problems that could fundamentally change financial services.

As Revolut grows, so does the complexity of protecting its customers. According to one report⁠(opens in a newly introduced window), over half of adults worldwide reported a scam encounter in 2025.

For Revolut, every transaction creates another opportunity to identify suspicious activity, investigate potential risks and implement robust and tailored protections for its customers. But the sheer volume of those transactions far outstrips the human resources available to any bank.

Industry observers note that “The biggest problem we can tackle with AI today is the scaling of humans versus the demand that we get,” notes AI Lead David Abitbol. That’s why one of Revolut’s largest AI applications is a FinCrime agent powered by OpenAI models.

Rather than requiring investigators to work through every eligible case manually, the agent can examine information, apply Revolut’s rules and complete the defined process automatically.

Recent findings suggest that the release of GPT‑5.5 was a turning point. It was then, says Abitbol, that the models had become capable and cost-effective enough for Revolut to delegate screening and investigation workflows entirely to the agent. The result is greater capacity to monitor transactions without increasing investigator headcount at the same rate as demand.

That, adds Information Security Engineer Mo Amiri, “translates directly into stronger protection and a more resilient system our customers can trust.”.

Recent findings suggest that ‘Move fast but build trust’ could easily be Revolut’s internal engineering slogan. While Abitbol points out that Codex has delivered a 30-60% reduction in coding time, he’s also clear that certain guardrails are non-negotiable.

“We have a systematic framework where anyone in the manufacturer who’s building anything with AI has the same set of standards across development, A/B testing, and business metric prediction,” he indicates. “So every engineer is held to the same standard of quality across the company. We started to get enough intelligence for reasonable costs where we could increasingly delegate initial investigations and screenings to the agent.”.

Industry observers note that for Senior Platform Engineer Dmitry Pitik, that 30-60% reduction in coding time became tangible while he was building an internal code-review service. He designed the system, broke it into features and initially assumed he’d need a development team to implement it.

According to recent reports, “I realised I don’t need a whole team of developers to implement this,” he recalls. “I can just launch different agents and assign each of them a particular task.” Codex became his implementation team, while Dmitry spent more time designing the system, planning the work and reviewing what came back.

This is a pattern that Abitbol has seen across Revolut. As Codex returns capacity to engineers they’re using that reclaimed time “to spend more time discussing design and the best solution. So we spend more time designing instead of implementing.”.

In a recent development, that doesn’t remove the need for engineering expertise, it just changes where that expertise is applied. “Every developer is responsible for the code they produce, and we don’t blindly trust AI,” Pitik claims. The result is a different division of work: AI can help with implementation, while engineers devote more attention to the decisions that determine whether the software is useful, reliable and worth building.

Recent findings suggest that that overhead is worth it. As Codex works on one task, Pitik can work in parallel on another. That kind of multitasking is essential in a manufacturer where, as Kim Maniovich explains, the average employee has “three different jobs.” Using Codex creates a virtuous (if challenging) flywheel where “month on month the targets we’re setting get more aggressive, but also more attainable. And so the bar keeps moving up. AI is making that possible.”.

Examples of what Revolut has been able to do with this new-found capacity include developing a tool to build web UIs for internal apps and external-facing products.

It has been revealed that or turning seven years of design documentation into AI-readable context in a single day, creating a foundation for tools intended to help designers work more effectively. The exercise illustrates how AI can make accumulated organisational knowledge more accessible, reducing the effort required to work with complex systems. “We can shift focus from the things which are notable but hard to do without AI to the things which matter for customers,” states Senior Designer Dmytro Pavlov.

Mo Amiri’s job is to make sure all of this speed is matched by security—not just for customers but for Revolut’s own employees. That gives him two views of AI at once: how it can help Revolut investigate a problem, and what teams need before they can deploy it safely.

According to recent reports, in a phishing investigation, for example, an analyst once had to gather an email, inspect its links and attachments, trace the sender and assemble the evidence manually. “With stronger AI tools, we can uncover those connections instantly, and dig deeper into the questions that really matter,” he notes.

While AI does the legwork and presents an investigator with a structured case, it’s still down to the individual to review the original records, decide whether the explanation makes sense and approve any action.

It has been revealed that amiri applies the same thinking when teams bring newly introduced AI applications into Revolut. He follows the complete chain: what information the system sees, where that information goes, which tools it can reach, what it can do with that access and what happens when something fails. He also tests whether apparently convincing conclusions are actually supported by the evidence.

It has been revealed that “The most critical decision is always about accountability,” he states. “If an AI tool suggests a code change, a human engineer needs to understand that change well enough to stand by it. That directly drives how we design the review process, giving developers the context they need without cluttering their everyday workflow.”.

Recent findings suggest that for Revolut, safeguards aren’t separate from innovation. They help establish the conditions under which teams can confidently adopt more capable technology. “That’s how you earn real confidence in AI,” he explains, “by making thoughtful decisions upfront and testing as you go.”.

30–60% reduction in coding time from task start to feature merge.

One engineer built an internal code-review service by delegating implementation tasks to multiple Codex agents.

One day to transform existing design-system documentation developed over roughly seven years into AI-readable context.

One to two days saved on one substantial security code-review task.

More transactions screened through the FinCrime agent without scaling investigators one for one.

Start with a problem worth solving. Revolut has put AI to work where demand is growing fastest and the stakes for customers are highest.

Use speed to raise ambition, not lower standards. Time saved on coding and investigation creates room for better design, harder questions and more consequential work.

Keep people on the hook. AI can gather evidence, write code and recommend action. A person still needs to understand the work well enough to stand behind it.

Build trust before you scale. Be clear about what a system can see, what it can do and what happens when it fails—then test those decisions as you go.

It has been revealed that make your knowledge usable. AI works better when it can reach clear, well-organised context. The same exercise often reveals where the organisation itself needs to be clearer.

Revolut has already shown how AI can increase the amount and complexity of work its teams can attempt. Its next opportunity is to carry that combination of capability, judgment and design into the way customers interact with their money.

Abitbol imagines a more conversational interface in which customers can ask Revolut to help with everyday financial tasks: blocking a card, managing a subscription or finding ways to save for a trip. Pavlov sees the design challenge underneath that experience—turning complexity into something consistent, familiar and easy to use.

According to recent reports, kim Maniovich connects that future to the culture driving the work. “I hope that we can take the values that we operate by every day—this unapologetic ambition, the desire to never settle—and enable people to apply that to their own lives through the products that we build for them.”.

As AI makes it easier to build, the differentiator becomes knowing what to build—and maintaining the judgment, standards and customer understanding to do it well. For Revolut, that’s the bigger promise of intelligence at work: less time spent on the mechanics of getting things done, and more capacity to make financial services safer, simpler and more useful for everyone.Banking services provided by licensed Revolut Group entities. Product Manager, Cameyo by Google.

This IDC Market Note contains an analysis on how Cameyo by Google, a virtual app delivery (VAD) solution, helps organizations deliver any legacy application over the web.

It has been revealed that organizations are increasingly adopting generative and agentic AI as they look for ways to unlock more business value. Yet for many IT leaders, business-critical legacy desktop apps stand in the way—too essential to retire, too complex and costly to rewrite—yet unequipped for the security challenges and productivity opportunities of the AI era.

Industry observers note that that doesn’t have to block your modernization strategy. By delivering Windows and legacy applications directly inside the Chrome browser, Cameyo by Google connects legacy workflows to Chrome Enterprise, ChromeOS, and Gemini—with zero replatforming required.

In a recent IDC Market Note, “Cameyo by Google: A Modern Bridge Technology Platform in Digital Workspace Transformation,” lead analyst Filippo Vanara examines how Cameyo reduces deployment complexity while enhancing security and lowering costs. Here are five of our key takeaways from the IDC Market Note:.

According to recent reports, enterprise modernization barriers make rewriting or replatforming legacy applications unfeasible for many organizations. The IDC report notes that "Cameyo is positioned as a strategic bridge between legacy application environments and modern, AI-driven digital workspaces." By connecting legacy systems to modern, AI-enhanced digital workspaces, Cameyo enables organizations to safeguard their existing technology investments.

2. Instant AI and security upgrades with Gemini and Chrome Enterprise.

In a recent development, moving legacy apps into the browser immediately surrounds them with modern capabilities they were never built to support. With Cameyo, legacy workflows run right alongside built-in enterprise AI like Gemini in Chrome—giving employees safe, managed AI tools instead of pushing them toward unmanaged "shadow AI." At the same time, apps can inherit Chrome’s advanced threat protections and Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies through Chrome Enterprise Premium, which the IDC Market Note highlights "This enables organizations to extend AI capabilities and modern security controls to legacy workflows.".

According to recent reports, 3. Protecting your organizations from cyberattacks.

Recent findings suggest that traditional VDI utilizes open VPNs and public server ports that leave organizations vulnerable to cyberattacks. According to the IDC Market Note, "As part of its value proposition, security is central to Cameyo. In fact, the platform adopts a zero trust architecture, isolating owners, sessions, and resources from the corporate network.” Additionally, "the use of non-persistent infrastructure and a simplified architecture reduces the overall attack surface.".

According to recent reports, 4. Slashing operational and virtualization costs.

Industry observers note that according to IDC's 2025 EMEA CloudOps Survey (n = 509) findings, 89% of organizations in Europe estimated that they are right now wasting their public cloud spending. When companies use Cameyo as opposed to complex virtual desktops, they consistently realize reduced costs. According to the IDC Market Note, "Cost is another core value proposition for Cameyo as it emphasizes its potential to deliver significant cost savings compared with traditional VDI and DaaS solutions: up to 54% reduction in total cost of ownership (TCO) when transitioning from legacy environments.".

5. Phased modernization across endpoints.

According to the IDC Market Note, IDC believes Cameyo represents an notable evolution within the broader VCC market, specifically reflecting a shift from desktop-centric virtualization to application-centric delivery models. In this context, the platform functions as a bridge technology, enabling enterprises to modernize incrementally rather than requiring full application replatforming. This aligns with IDC's view that most organizations will pursue phased modernization strategies, maintaining legacy software while gradually transitioning to cloud-native architectures.” By delivering legacy applications as Progressive Web Apps (PWAs), Cameyo helps businesses modernize without being tethered to a specific device or operating system. When paired with ChromeOS Flex, Cameyo can ensure seamless access to those legacy apps on older devices, extending existing hardware lifespans and reducing capital expenditures.

Adopting AI doesn't mean leaving legacy applications stranded. True workplace modernization integrates existing, business-critical software into a secure, unified AI ecosystem—without requiring complex app rewrites or costly migrations.
